#1023. Ben White says England fans may not have booed him 'if they knew the full story' over squad exile

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

White walked out of the World Cup camp in Qatar and subsequently made himself unavailable for the rest of Sir Gareth Southgate’s time in charge

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Ben White believes England supporters would not boo him if they knew the complete story behind his departure from the 2022 World Cup squad.

However, the Arsenal defender maintains that he has no intention to "throw anyone under the bus" by speaking out about the incident.

White left the national camp in Qatar citing "personal reasons", following a reported fallout with assistant manager Steve Holland, and subsequently ruled himself out of selection for the remainder of Sir Gareth Southgate’s time in charge.

Though he returned under Thomas Tuchel in March, White was booed by supporters before injury ruled him out of this summer’s World Cup.

His comeback was eventful during a friendly against Uruguay, where he scored and later gave away a penalty.

“I think before the game, I was thinking, just don’t…not stand out, but just nice and easy, you know,” he added.

“Then I came on and obviously get booed. Then I score. Then I give away a pen. So it was obviously full of emotions that night, and it was a good night.

“Everyone can do whatever they want. You know, it’s fine with me. Whatever they want to do, and I think just think about maybe not knowing the full story.

The 29-year-old says he stands by his decision of four years ago, but is looking forward to his “story continuing”.

“It’s something that I’ve not spoken about, and I won’t go into detail about it,” White told talkSPORT. “Yes, it’s a decision that I don’t want to be talking about anyone negatively or throwing anyone under the bus.

“It was obviously not an ideal situation, and (a decision) that I probably still would make.

“There’s loads of things that happened and communication wasn’t great.

“It’s something that I don’t want to throw anyone under the bus. I think there’s a lot of people who tried to do that to me. So it’s something that I wouldn’t want to do to someone else.”

He added on BBC Radio 5 Live: “I don’t think I would (change decision).

“Obviously, I was a bit younger. I’m a bit older now. I think, as a person, I’m quite real, and I think I made the decision that I would probably continue to make.

“It’s one that I’m not happy about, but obviously it happened, it’s time to move on.

“It’s such a privilege to ever get close to playing for your country, something I probably didn’t even dream of because I didn’t think it would be anywhere near my reality.

“There’s been a few bumps, I’m obviously here now, and looking forward to this story continuing.”

The basis of White’s alleged falling out with Holland is thought to be over an interview where the Arsenal defender admitted to not watching football on television.

He said: “To be fair, I don’t. I don’t know if I actually said I don’t like it because people say I don’t like football, which is obviously not true.

“It’s because I don’t watch it, which I think is quite normal for someone who does a job and then doesn’t go home and then continue watching that job.

“But I think it’s my way of release from the game because it’s so intense, obviously.”

#1021. Merson: Man Utd transfer policy is to blame - not Carrick

Michael Carrick's future at Man Utd is in doubt with the club inside the Premier League relegation zone; Mauricio Pochettino would be open to talks with Man Utd if he was approached by club; Sky Sports' Paul Merson says he would be surprised if Carrick was sacked

Football Expert & Columnist @PaulMerse

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Sky Sports' Paul Merson believes Manchester United’s transfer strategy is to blame for their worst start to a top-flight season instead of head coach Michael Carrick.

Carrick's job is increasingly in doubt, with United sitting in the Premier League relegation zone after taking only eight points from their first 10 games, and Mauricio Pochettino is open to a discussion if approached.

One win in 11 games, 30 goals conceded in all competitions, the worst record of any team in the top-five European leagues and a club-worst start to a league season has ramped up the pressure on Carrick - but Merson feels he is not at fault.

"I just can't blame the manager. They change managers left, right and centre all the time and it's the same results," said Merson.

"It doesn't matter if you have Arsene Wenger, Sir Alex Ferguson, Pep Guardiola or Jose Mourinho sitting on the bench. The mistakes they are making are down to the players.

"If they weren't running around for the manager, they'd have been ripped to shreds by Roma and Aston Villa and they didn't. They came back in both of those games. I'd be quite surprised if they let Carrick go at the moment

"They got it the wrong way around with their transfer policy. The first window they went for buying forwards. The next window, they started bringing in midfield players and now at the end of the season, they're probably going to go and buy defenders.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"They should have gone with defenders first. You can't build a house on a puddle. You've got to have a strong defence and they haven't done that.

"They've done it completely the wrong way around and it's come back to bite them.

"They've got to look at themselves upstairs and think that they got this horribly wrong, not Michael Carrick."

United States head coach Pochettino could be set to return to the Premier League for the first time since leaving Chelsea in May 2024.

"He's got experience, major experience. He's worked in the Premier League a lot of times," said Merson. "If they get rid of Michael Carrick, they're not bringing someone in who's going to take six months to get used to the Premier League. This man's a top, top manager.

"I don't think Carrick could go, but if they could get Pochettino for £7m, that's a cheap deal. He's a good manager, but I think Michael Carrick can be a very good manager. They've just done it the wrong way round in all the transfer windows.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"Man Utd are not one of the biggest teams anymore, but they've still got one of the biggest expectations in football and that is the problem. I think Man United are, and this is no disrespect, a mid-table team.

"We keep on talking about Man United of 15 years ago. When they had Wayne Rooney, Cristiano Ronaldo and top draw players. It's not the case anymore.

"They're into buying players in the market who are a flip of a coin. They might be good, or they might not, and that's not how you do it at Man United. With the financial rules now, it's going to be difficult for them to get anywhere near back to where they were 15, 20, and 25 years ago.

"It's a great club and a massive club, but the expectations of managing that type of club, and where you've got to finish in the league, are very, very high, and I think that's what sometimes puts managers off."

#1020. Daily briefing: The ‘overshoot COP’ kicks off

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Scientists say that record-breaking wildfires this summer — such as this one in southwestern France — could mark a shift in southern Europe’s fire patterns because of hotter, dryer conditions. (Maximilien Lamy/AFP via Getty)

A troubling reality hangs over the United Nations climate conference (COP31) opening in Turkey today: overshoot. For the first time, the annual meeting of the world’s countries to hash out action on climate change must face the fact that it is now inevitable for global temperatures to exceed the 1.5 °C warming limit pledged in the Paris Agreement. Call it ‘the overshoot COP’. “We need to first recognize that global policy has failed. This is a moment of self-critique,” says climate scientist Johan Rockström.

Environmental journalist Fiona Harvey, who has been to almost every UN climate conference for more than 20 years, asks: what’s the point of COP? “The convention that all resolutions must pass by consensus has given bad actors free rein,” she writes. The Paris agreement itself has “reached an impasse”, not least because of the withdrawal of the United States. But China — the world’s biggest carbon emitter — is more engaged in multinational negotiations than ever, partly because of its huge stake in green technologies such as solar panels. And the impact of the UN process is everywhere, from the rise of electric cars to the energy transformation. “Any time you have a consensus decision, it sends a signal,” says Sue Biniaz, a former US climate negotiator. “These days with the geopolitics of the world — if something can be agreed by the whole world, it’s impactful.”

The estimated increase in peak warming this century that will be caused by the United States abandoning its net-zero target under President Donald Trump’s administration, if US policies don’t change. (Nature | 8 min read, from October)

A new artificial-intelligence system enables researchers to enhance the performance of robotic equipment in their labs. In the process, scientists describe their research programme and lab set-up to the AI agents, which generate step-by-step experimental protocols for the lab’s robots. The system can also generate a virtual version of the lab in which to test its suggestions, and even devise a new floor plan that optimizes the placement of lab robots and equipment. The “very cool” concept could drastically reduce the effort required to set up automated labs, says bioengineer Evan Collins.

Reference: arXiv preprint (not peer reviewed)

People seem to find conversations more enjoyable if they contain more pink noise — sound in which there is equal energy per octave of frequency. Researchers analysed 1,000 conversations between strangers and found that participants felt a stronger sense of connection with their partner when their chats had featured more pink noise. The team also found that chats between podcast hosts comprise more pink noise as the series continues, which suggests that making a conversation ‘pinker’ is a skill that can be honed, says psychologist and study co-author Kathryn O’Nell.

A separate research team found that pink noise can also help to kickstart the brain’s ‘wash cycle’ during sleep. They found that timing bursts of pink noise to ‘slow’ brain waves can encourage cerebrospinal fluid to flow through the brain, clearing out any harmful particles that have accumulated during waking hours. The team says that the pink pulses might activate a particular kind of slow wave that silences distractions.

The Guardian | 4 min read & Scientific American | 4 min read

Reference: Science Advances paper & Science Translational Medicine paper

In his new book, On the Equality of All Things, physicist Carlo Rovelli writes that fundamental physics is overrated. “It’s great science,” he tells Nature. “But stop thinking that it is the root of everything else.” Physics also has a hubris problem, he says, which can lead to wild goose chases for evidence of phenomena that aren’t real. Discoveries in quantum mechanics and general relativity have brought us to the cusp of fresh conceptual breakthroughs, but it might take some time for a coherent picture to emerge from the noise, he says.

Compared to the dangers of extreme weather, “little attention has been given to what happens when El Niño disrupts food supplies, affects what people eat and potentially changes their exposure to infectious disease,” argue economist Eoin McLaughlin and management scholar Matthias Beck. “One advantage with El Niño is that there is plenty of warning,” they note, urging governments and agencies to prepare for the weather pattern’s possible effects on food and health systems.

Some men looking for emotional support are turning to commercial chatbots and specially designed AI apps, partly because of the stigma around traditional mental health treatment. “You don’t have to make an appointment. You don’t have to go sit in a waiting room. You don’t have to even really explicitly take that initial step to ask for help,” notes psychiatrist Michael Heinz. But is therapy-like discussion with an AI system better than no therapy at all? “I think [AI app] founders have to realize therapy does have a rate of harm,” says psychiatrist John Torous, who specializes in digital mental health. “You need some rules of the road.”

STAT | 17 min read (free registration required)

The PRETTY CubeSat, which is run by a consortium including the European Space Agency, became the first satellite to understand and obey a spoken command when radio amateurs in Norway sent a signal to launch the video game Doom. (Space.com | 7 min read)

Read more: How the classic computer game Doom became a tool for science (Nature | 6 min read, from March)

#1019. Michael Carrick takes training as Man Utd hierarchy ponders his future

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Carrick’s future is still up in the air with Mauricio Pochettino a top contender to replace him

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Michael Carrick took training on Tuesday as Manchester United’s powerbrokers drag their heels over the beleaguered head coach’s future ahead of a key meeting in Monaco.

The former midfielder’s days in charge appear to be numbered after overseeing the club’s worst start to a campaign since 1986, leaving the Red Devils in the relegation zone over the international break.

United, who languish in 18th, are using the two-week hiatus to review Carrick’s position and consider alternatives, with the head coach widely expected to lose his job following discussions.

But Old Trafford sources remained adamant on Tuesday lunchtime that no decision had been made after the 45-year-old reported to the Carrington training complex earlier that day to take training.

Carrick’s future is set to be decided 800 miles away from Manchester in Monaco, where director of football Jason Wilcox and chief executive Omar Berrada are due to give their views to United’s ownership.

A meeting is reportedly scheduled in the principality on Wednesday with co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, whose Ineos company controls football operations and would sign off a change at the top with the Glazers.

United are keeping tight-lipped on the process and relevant meetings, which is only prolonging the agony for popular former midfielder Carrick, who made 464 appearances for the club between 2006 and 2018.

Mauricio Pochettino, the former Tottenham, Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea boss, has emerged as the leading contender to replace him.

The former Argentina international has held talks with United in the past and is understood to be interested in the Old Trafford post, but hefty compensation would be due for the United States boss.

Just three months ago Pochettino and his staff extended their deals until 2030 and are currently in Georgia preparing for Nations League quarter-final fixtures against Haiti on Saturday and Tuesday.

Aston Villa boss Unai Emery is admired, while ex-Newcastle boss Eddie Howe and former Germany head coach Julian Nagelsmann were linked a fortnight ago when United seriously considered replacing Carrick.

A 4-1 Champions League loss at Como and 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth left the head coach’s job hanging by a thread, but the club decided to give him the opportunity to turn the situation around.

Carrick’s side subsequently lost 2-0 at Chelsea, where they were unable to take their chances and saw Lisandro Martinez sent off, before last Tuesday’s thrilling 3-2 Champions League comeback win against Roma.

A scarcely believable 4-4 draw against Aston Villa followed on Sunday, after which the head coach stressed he would not walk away and was looking to the international break as usual.

“It’s been a right mixed week or two or three, really, if you’re looking at the events,” Carrick said. “But I’m pretty clear where we need to go and how we need to get there.

“Obviously some of the boys will be flying off around the world and different things, and the group will be split for 10 days or so.

“But as a normal international week is, you know, we’ll have some training. We’ll have one or two days off, but not too much. But we’ll train, and we’ll get ready for the next game.”

United return to action with a Premier League trip to rivals Liverpool on 22 November.

#1018. Chelsea bullied by Brian Brobbey and Sunderland

Talk about cramming everything in. Brian Brobbey only played for 67 minutes but, in that time, he collected a yellow card, ripped Levi Colwill’s shirt and earned himself a standing ovation after morphing into a battering ram.

Régis Le Bris, Sunderland’s head coach, said there was nobody like the Netherlands striker in the Premier League and it said everything that everyone wanted to make Brobbey centre of attention after a long overdue home win, even though he had not scored. Everyone, that is, bar Xabi Alonso.

“No, he’s not unstoppable,” Chelsea’s head coach replied when asked why his team had found Brobbey too much to handle. “He’s stoppable – but only when you defend better than we did. We were not bullied. We didn’t produce enough.”

That is one way of putting it. Another would be to say Brobbey was everything that Chelsea, much to Alonso’s disgust, were not: a bristling menace, a steamroller wearing a pair of boots, a player on a mission to help transform the mood – Enzo Le Fée’s decisive spot kick owed everything to Brobbey.

Chelsea arrived on Wearside looking to establish themselves in the top four ahead of the break but, instead, Alonso watched through his fingers as Sunderland reminded everyone why they were the joyous story of last season, a beautiful mix of inspiration and perspiration.

In fairness to the Chelsea manager, he refused to get caught in the minutiae of contentious penalty decisions – one that Chelsea were denied, another that they conceded – and could only lament as Sunderland ground out their first Premier League win since August 30, 70 long days ago.

“It wasn’t the best game,” Alonso said. “I think that we didn’t deserve more than probably one point, maybe. We need to be more consistent on the move, to get the ball from one side to the other, and we didn’t do that good enough. We didn’t produce enough to deserve to win.”

Unlike Sunderland. If you had turned up at the Stadium of Light without looking at the Premier League table, you would not have believed the hosts were bottom and you would not have given credence to the idea Le Bris, who has worked miracles these past two years, was under pressure.

Things, however, could not have started worse for Le Bris. Though Granit Xhaka has not shown last season’s form in these challenging opening months, the game plan was built around him, so to see the Sunderland captain hobbling off after three minutes was symptomatic of how things have gone for the Wearsiders.

“He felt something in the final sprint of the warm-up,” Le Bris explained. “We don’t know how bad it is.”

He is not the kind of coach, though, who will bemoan bad fortune. Le Bris sent on Jules Ahoka to replace Xhaka and watched as he, along with colleagues in red and white, set about trampling all over Chelsea’s intentions with incessant hard work.

Yet there was more to it. Sunderland can play, either intricately or directly, and a lovely move in the 12th minute needed a desperate, sliding intervention from Pep Chavarría’s to stop Trai Hume’s volley sliding in at the far post.

In the next attack, another Chemsdine Talbi cross – the Moroccan having been found by a peach of a pass from goalkeeper Robin Roefs – invited Brobbey to inflict maximum damage, but the Dutchman made a hash of his opportunity.

So close for Brobbey! 🤏 Sunderland almost take the lead against Chelsea. https://t.co/CUE6jHbPH2

The momentum could have changed completely in the 23rd minute. Alonso, his players and staff were convinced they would be given a penalty after Cole Palmer tumbled when his legs tangled with Luke O’Nien but, after a lengthy delay, VAR Nick Hopton felt there was no case to answer.

Hopton was involved again in the 33rd minute but, as Alonso said, Chelsea only had themselves to blame. Colwill simply could not contain Brobbey when he began marauding, grappling, grabbing and clipping the Dutchman’s heels. Le Fée did the rest, sending Mike Penders the wrong way.

Enzo Le Fee dispatches the penalty as Sunderland take the lead against Chelsea! 🔴⚪️ https://t.co/cCtYsHVWB9

From that point, Chelsea were in trouble, no matter how many changes Alonso made. They huffed, puffed, but nothing worked. They had come up against a red-and-white wall, fortified by constant backing from the stands, and the west Londoners were never going to knock it down.

One incident, as the clock ticked towards 90 minutes, encapsulated everything good about this Sunderland display when O’Nien chased down substitute Geovany Quenda to make a challenge. Another moment of defending from Thomas Meunier on Morgan Rogers was exceptional.

“You could see our identity and our togetherness and the way we managed the game,” said Le Bris, who was booked when hectoring referee Jarred Gillett. “These three points were critical. It was a struggle at times to manage situations. We showed as a group real heart.”

And nobody did that more than Brobbey. No wonder Le Bris will be hoping Xavi Hernández, the Netherlands head coach, handles him with care over the next 10 days. On this form, he will be the fuel that drives Sunderland’s quest for survival.

“You know when you come here in this stadium it will be a difficult game and that was the matter tonight. We knew it would be tough, we are disappointed we lost the game. At one point it went very fast from side to side. Sometimes we had to control. With 11 behind the ball it is difficult to find the spaces.”

On where Chelsea stand ahead of the international break...

“How you do – good or not – it is a matter of staying together. The international break is coming so the lads can be calm in the head and when we all come back we need to be motivated to go again.”

“For me it wasn’t a penalty. He barely touched him, I think it was the other way round. He grabbed him.”

They cannot make anything of set piece and Sunderland have the three points - it wasn’t pretty but they needed the three points and edged the contest.

Questions will be asked of Chelsea now, they were bullied in the first-half and weren’t able to create anything in the second.

Chelsea with the ball inside the Sunderland half. The visitors bring Rogers down and Chelsea have a free-kick. Last-chance sallon for the west Londoners...

Sunderland have a throw inside the Chelsea half - this is about game management for the side in dire need of a win now...

Angulo nrings down his man after a poor pass from Sadiki. The visitors with a free-kick inside their own half.

Emegha drifts past Mukiele before he feels the full force of a Luke O’Nein tackle. It looks as though he gets the ball but the ref awards the free-kick. It’s in the final third, can Chelsea create anything from this?

In short ‘yes’, Estevao delivers a peach of a ball and Welbeck gets on the end of it. BUT his header is over, when it seemed easier to hit the target.

Sunderland in Chelsea half, they’re looking for a free-kick as Angulo goes down. The referee isn’t having any of it...

Sunderland break at pace (only the second time this half) Isador finds Talbi who is free before cutting inside and unleashing a shot from outside the box. It’s just wide, don’t think it was too far away though.

Talbi is off for Angulo, Rigg on for Le Fee for Sunderland, and for Chelsea, Henderson makes way for Emegha.

For all their possession this half Chelsea have not forced Roefs into a meaningful save. The west Londoners are again dominating possession in and near the hinterland of the Sunderland box, but it’s all a bit after you Claude and ultimately Roefs gladly picks up an anaemic cross. That sums up Chelsea as an attacking force today.

Chelsea corner after Geovany Quenda gets in a shot from the left-side of the area that gets a tiny hint of a deflection. Roefs punches away the set-piece and Sunderland breathe a sigh of relief.

Better from Sunderland, there are spaces in behind Chelsea as the visitors go in search of the equaliser and over the past few minutes the hosts have found them.

Lovely ball from Reinildo finds Sadiki in space on the left, they keep the ball brilliantly before Le Fee plays in Isador, it’s a one-on-one and all the Frenchman has to do it dink it over the on-rushing keeper. He goes low, however, and Penders makes a fine save - that was the game for Sunderland there...Penders has kept Chelsea in this.

Brobbey may have been tiring but without him Sunderland cannot keep the ball. Sadiki earns a free-kick which takes a bit of pressure off the hosts.

Palmer pulls back for Gusto whose dinky, cheeky chip tries to find Roefs off his line. He doesn’t succeed and the Dutch goalkeeper claims with ease.

Chelsea still seeing plenty of the ball, Sunderland may well be tiring. It’s hard to keep up that intensity for 90 minutes, hence Isador on for Brobbey, but they are struggling to keep the ball at the moment.

The first half was lively and entertaining, this half has been lively and lacking in anything that could be remotely described as a spectacle...

Rogers tries to find Palmer, but the ball is too long and Roefs gobbles up with ease.

Meanwhile, Hume looks injured and Chelsea do not give the ball back after Sunderland kicked it off. You won’t be shocked to hear that the home fans are not happy with that...

Change for Sunderland, Brobbey off for Isador. The Dutchman has been brilliant today, he might have scored a couple of goals, but despite not finding the back of the net he has proved a handful for the Chelsea backline. I would have kept him on for longer...

Chelsea looking better this half, they’re seeing plenty of the ball but have not had a shot on goal since the break. In fact there have only been two touches in either box this 45...Sunderland won’t mind that at 1-0.

ON - Welbeck and GustoOFF - Neto and Palestra

So Alonso has opted for a physical presence up front.

No sooner had I pressed send on that last post than Chelsea break through the middle but some great last-ditch defending from Muenier prevents Estevao from getting a shot at goal.

Chelsea haven’t been able to play through Sunderland and you think they’d need to bring on a physical presence up front if that’s to change.

Another chance for Sunderland - they break down the right before Hume sends in a low ball to the penalty box, it’s met first time by Le Fee, I think, and Penders saves low to his right. To state the obvious, the hosts would love a second to give them a deserved cushion. As I typed that last but the linesman has his flag up, it wouldn’t have counted, promising signs nonetheless.

Pressure from Sunderland. A good bit of possession ends with Mukiele swinging in a lovely cross from the right which Chelsea are forced to head clear for a corner. Nothing results from the set piece, but things still looking promising for Sunderland who look as energetic and ‘at it’ as they did in the first half.

Rogers picks up the ball in the middle just inside the Sunderland half and is immediately pick-pocketed by one of three Sunderland players. The Chelsea men have not been allowed to settle when they have a sniff of a mini counter.

Good, feisty opening to this half, Chelsea look more up for it, though to be fair they couldn’t look any more insipid than they did in the first 45. Meanwhile, Brobbey shoves Lavia and earns a yellow. Think that’s three yellows for the hosts now.

It is going to be fascinating to see how a team with well known - and long standing - disciplinary issues copes with a pressurised pursuit of an equaliser. There have already been a couple of flash points that Chelsea’s players have reacted to and it wouldn’t be the wildest thing to predict referee Jarred Gillett brandishing a red card before the end of the game. Watch it unfold with interest.

Brobbey lays the ball off for Meunier in the final third, it’s asking a lot of the Belgian but his compounds the Dutchman’s error with one of his own - stretching for the ball and taking out Caicedo. Something for which he earns a needless yellow card.

There’s a bit of argy bargy on the pitch, not sure what started that but the referee Jarred Gillett has to have a word with several players. All a bit of handbags really.

They’re back under way on the banks of the Wear. Chelsea have been insipid and you imagine they won’t be as bed these next 45 minutes. Can Sunderland play with the same aggression and energy? We’re about to find out.

Changes Estevao on for Colwill, interesting substitution to say the least...

So close for Brobbey! 🤏 Sunderland almost take the lead against Chelsea. https://t.co/CUE6jHbPH2

The half ends with an audacious attempt at goal from Rogers, a full 40 yards out from a free kick. It’s catching practice for Roefs and that sums up Chelsea as an attacking force in the first 45. Sunderland are well worth their lead.

Rogers has a shot-cum-cross from the left and it sails high, wide and not so handsome. He’s been on the periphery this half, as has Palmer and that explains as much as anything why they are behind. Sunderland have cut out the supply to him and Roefs has had little to do as a result.

Approaching half-time and save for the contentious VAR call when he wanted a penalty, Cole Palmer has done absolutely nothing. The talk of him being in the England squad, on this evidence, is for the birds. Sunderland are full value for their half-time lead. Chelsea, like Palmer, have been absolutely insipid.

There will be five minutes added time in this first half.

Something I’ve not written much this half ‘chance for Chelsea’. Neto works a bit of space in the inside-right channel outside the box, but his shot is easily saved by Roefs.

Talbi attacks down the left but cuts in when he would have been better served going wide.

Chelsea have seen plenty of the ball but they’ve been way too slow and cumbersome with it. It’s been in front of the Sunderland back lines and easy to defend against. The hosts are letting the visitors have the ball wide and with Neto in the middle, it’s been too easy for Le Bris’s men.

Brobbey wants the ball at every opportunity and Sunderland would be well advised to give it to him. Colwill is has his hands full.

Sunderland have kept the aggression and energy throughout the half - and kept Chelsea quiet as a result. As I type that the hosts give Lavia too much room 25 yards out and his shot is well wide of the left-hand post.

The lead is no more than Sunderland deserve and that means, as the table stands, Manchester United are bottom of the Premier League. Fair play to Enzo Le Fee for keeping his nerve in a pressure situation. Sunderland needed him to be cool.

They’ve deserved that, they’ve been the better side and are well worth the lead. Le Fee sends Penders the wrong way, burying the ball into the bottom left corner.

Brobbey has been a handful (as he always is) and Colwill brings the BIG (yes, caps lock and bold are necessary) Dutchman down in the box. It looks as though it was six of one and hald a dozen of the other, but the spotkick stands.

Ahoka has impressed since coming on, his nifty footwork helps win Sunderland a throw in the final third. Mukiele has a big thrown on him but it does not result in a chance. Still, this is good from the hosts and Chelsea are second best at the moment. They were in the first half against United last week, and ended up winning so...

Another chance for Sunderland as Brobbey bullies Colwill on the halfway line before driving at Fofana. He gets to the edge of the area, beats the Chelsea defender before his shot goes wide. The last touch took him too wide, but again, promising signs for the hosts.

Early days this, of course, but Sunderland absolutely do not look like a team that is currently the worst in the Premier League. They should have the lead here but Brian Brobbey’s miss from six yards is indicative of how things have been going.

Sunderland are being aggressive, they need to be and it’s a contrast from the previous month. With that approach, however, comes risks and Mukiele gives away a free-kick inside his own half. Luckily for him, nothing comes from the set-piece.

First chance of the game for Chelsea and, as with Brobbey 10 minutes ago, it should have found the back of the net. Rogers is the culprit - he sends his header wide of the right post after a grade-A cross from Palestra.

One-all in terms of great chances...but the score remains 0-0.

Palmer is bundled over on the outskirts of the area and he and Chelsea players appeal for something - could be a free-kick of penalty...the referee is having nothing of it. The replay suggests he may well have been hard done by but VAR also is having nothing of it...it was a foul as none of the marauding Sunderland players, O’Nien among them (obviously), got the ball and most definitely got Palmer...think the hosts got away with that one.

Yellow card for Ahoka for a foul on Caicado, he may need to walk a tightrope for the rest of the match. But it’s an illustration of the energy and purpose with which Sunderland have approached this match.

Sunderland have looked the better side so far and have had the better chances.

Better from Chelsea in the sense that they controlled the game for two minutes. Lots of good, neat passing but no end product, it’s all in front of a composed Sunderland defence.

Another good chance for Sunderland and once again Talbi proves his worth. He cuts back onto his right and delivers a peach of a cross from the left. Brobbey gets in front of his man and all he has to do is hit the target...alas his first-time shot goes wide. That should be 1-0 to the hosts who are the better side at the moment.

Good from Sunderland who look so much more energetic than at any point during their previous few matches. Ahoka does well in the middle before freeing Talbi down the left. The Moroccan gets in a cross and Le Fee’s shot is blocked. Promising signs for the hosts.

What a blow this is for Regis Le Bris. Less than two minutes gone and Granit Xhaka is having to leave the pitch with an obvious injury. Some fans around the press box booed Xhaka as he was hobbling off - is that a hangover from his attempts to move to Chelsea? - but on afternoon when Le Bris needed everything to go his way, he’s already on the back foot.

Neto is in the Sunderland half but three Sunderland players snap at his heels like a hyperactive dog after a bone. Chelsea haven’t been allowed to settle yet. Plenty of time to go though...

Sunderland are looking to find Brobbey at every opportunity, but Chelsea’s backline intercept well. Nothing of note created so far, but the hosts are on the front foot, which is what they and the fans needed.

Sunderland attack down the right with Meunier, nothing comes of it but the hosts look as though they mean business here. A minute later Sadiki and Brobbey nearly combine to create something. Close but no cigar...

Bad news for Sunderland, Xhaka is down and it looks as though he may well have to come off...oh dear. While he’s not been at his best this season he’s still the man the side looks towards for inspiration (an boy do they need that is dollops today...)...and, indeed he is forced off. Ahoka, who is highly rated but raw replaces him. The Congolese player now has a big chance to make a name for himself.

Chelsea with the early possession, but they go backwards and the hosts are up and at them with the press and the visitors have to go back to Penders in goal.

They’re under way at the Stadium of Light, Sunderland are in their famous red and white and Chelsea in their away outfit of black shirts and shorts and yelow socks.

As the Stadium of Light remembers all those who lost their lives in war.

The Last Post is played and the minute’s silence is impeccably observed.

Warming-up in our Remembrance shirt ❤️ https://t.co/aTB8sfdLKP

And we’re moments away from kick-off in the North East.

This is a big afternoon for both teams. It will be an emotional one, too, for Jordan Henderson, who started his career at Sunderland many years ago. Xabi Alonso has confirmed he has been picked because of the quality he provides, rather than any sentimental value, and Regis Le Bris revealed ahead of the fixture he tried to bring the England international home during the summer window, when Chelsea attempted to sign Granit Xhaka.

“Jordan is a great player, first of all,” said Le Bris. “For the connection with the club, it’s not my part. It was with Flo [Ghisolfi, director of football] and Kyril [Louis-Dreyfus, the Sunderland owner], they had conversations.

“I thought that it could have been a good signing for the club, a good symbol, a great player, a great leader. But the market is the market.”

Has just said that Sunderland, and in particular Brian Brobbey, can ‘get at’ the Chelsea defence of Palestra, Fofana, Colwill, Chavarria. I am not sure he has seen much of the Sunderland attack this year, but Brobbey is a handful for any defence.

“We have to stay consistent and true to our identity. It’s always difficult to predict what the other side does but you have to focus on yourself and connect with the fans and impose our ideas.”

On whether they can get a result today...

“I hope so... I see the players every day, they care and sometime its hard to understand the unforced errors.”

“He’s loved by fans and team, so we know the situation at beginning of season. He is an important player for us and didn’t start for various reasons, but has qualities run in behind and finish - he’s excited worked and has worked hard.”

I mentioned earlier that Sunderland did the double over Chelsea last season. But the manner of the victories revealed more than the scorelines. In both matches, especially the second, the west Londoners looked somewhat lightweight and easily bullied.

This season Xabi Alonso has been determined to ensure that that is not the case this season.

In the land of the Premier League giants, Chelsea have been on the small side in recent seasons. But they are no longer being looked down upon and are finally showing signs of being capable of going toe-to-toe physically with opponents.

Sunday’s opponents Sunderland ran Chelsea off the park twice last season. Only once, in the 36th Premier League game of the campaign against Liverpool, did Chelsea cover more distance than their opposition.

Here’s Matt Law’s article on Why Chelsea have gone from pint-sized players to taller trees...

SUNDERLAND XI TO FACE CHELSEA: Roefs, Meunier, Mukiele, O’Nein, Reinildo, Xhaka, Hume, Le Fee, Talbi, Brobbey.

Subs: Ellborg, Danso, Methalie, Rigg, Tutierov, Ahoka, Fofana, Angulo, Isador

Regis Le Bris makes two changes from the sorry defeat at Coventry City. Nordi Mukiele returns to the centre of defence and there’s a start for Chemsdine Talbi  – Chris Rigg and Nilson Angulo are the ones to make way.

CHELSEA XI TO FACE SUNDERLAND: Penders, Palestra, Fofana, Colwill, Chavarria, Henderson, Lavia, Caicedo, Neto, Palmer, Rogers.

Subs: Sharman-Lowe, Gusto, Anselmino, Nicoll-Jazuli, Barco, Quenda, Estevao, Welbeck, Emegha.

Xabi Alonso also makes two changes – Pep Chavarria and Jordan Henderson start today. Estevao Willian drops to the bench while Josh Acheampong is a somewhat surprise absence the 20.

Goalkeeper Mike Penders continues in goal with Emiliano Martinez deemed not ready to return having fractured his jaw against Everton.

That Sunderland did the double over Chelsea last season.

A last-minute winner from Chemsdine Talbi grabbed the points at Stamford Bridge, before Sunderland won 2-1, without breaking sweat, at the Stadium of Light on the last day of the campaign.

Those victories, and the manner of them, underlined what a season it was for Regis Le Bris’s men. How they wish this campaign started as that one ended.

RLB's XI to take on Chelsea! 📝👊 #SUNCHE https://t.co/1XWyHk0x56

Your Chelsea side today! ✔️ #CFC | #SUNCHE https://t.co/ciaILJeAuu

For Sunderland that argument is easy to make – they are bottom of the Premier League, are without a win since August and for morale, if nothing else need at least a point, though three is really what the doctor orders.

For Chelsea – fourth in the table and with three wins in their past four league outings – the argument that this is a must-win game is harder to make, but bear with me here...

Facing a Sunderland team who are suffering from the worst of both worlds – blunt in attack and pitiful in defence (what a difference from last season...) and have proven all too easy to beat (as their 2-0 home defeat Zagreb illustrated on Thursday) – the west Londoners are expected to win. Fail to return to the capital with the three points and there will once again be question marks over Xabi Alonso’s side. They are flaky and flashy in equal measure, able to play and win well in spurts, but once again unable to mount sustained pressure needed for a title challenge and forced to battle it out for the hope of a top-four spot at best. Those will be the arguments raised should they not win this afternoon.

The hosts doubtless wish that their ‘issues’ were as golden as today’s opposition. For Trai Hume, who scored in this fixture last season, the Sunderland players are at fault for the sorry start to the season and he wants to put right the wrongs so far, starting today.

“I couldn’t tell you what’s changed. We thought we’d addressed it after the Leeds game, where we were aggressive, strong, but we go out there tonight and see the old habits of the start of the season. Everything’s a bit laboured, and it’s something the staff can’t fix, it’s on us as players,” Hume said.

“We’re still together as a club, as a team. I think the run of form we’re on, it would be easy to think we’re not, but we are. We are really upset with how we’ve been playing, and the results don’t lie. We haven’t been good enough and we know that. We have to address that.”

Kevin De Bruyne to Everton is on, with the Manchester City legend struggling at Napoli

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Everton have launched a shock bid for former Manchester City man, Kevin De Bruyne.

The Belgian is a legend of the Premier League, having won six titles and racked up an in while racking up almost 200 goal involvements in 288 appearances in the English top flight – but since leaving the Etihad, things haven't been as rosy for him in Italian football.

Now, Everton are prepared to offer the 35-year-old a return to the northwest of England in one of the biggest-name moves of the Toffees' recent history.

De Bruyne spent 10 years at Manchester City before swapping one blue shirt for another and signing for Napoli last summer.

The playmaker has struggled to make a difference in Serie A, however, with Calciomercato reporting that he “appears to be in a decline mentally and could sensationally return to the Premier League in January.”

The report notes that Everton are making a sensational swoop to bring De Bruyne back to England and have already made contact with the player's entourage.

The Merseysiders are up to sixth in the Premier League at the moment and enjoying a good season, despite leaving themselves short over the summer in terms of transfer business.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Fans were disappointed when the club sold striker Beto without a replacement – leaving Thierno Barry as the only recognised No.9 at the Hill Dickinson Stadium – while a failure to replace long-serving right-back Seamus Coleman after his retirement has meant that midfielder Merlin Rohl has taken the role on this term.

There has been recent uncertainty regarding the loan spell of Jack Grealish, too, with the England international dropped by manager David Moyes after breaching the club's disciplinary rules when he reportedly skipped training.

Grealish – who is on loan from Man City, incidentally – has very little chance of joining the Toffees permanently now, with some suggesting that his loan spell could be curtailed in January.

De Bruyne's contract runs until 2027, with the Partenopei holding an option for another year.

Whether club president Aurelio De Laurentiis decides to release the player midseason remains another matter.

The 35-year-old is worth €8 million, as per Transfermarkt. Everton travel away to Brentford when Premier League action resumes after the international break.

#1016. Virgil van Dijk 'not in any panic' over Liverpool contract talks

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The centre-back’s contract expires next June and talks have not yet been held on his future

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Virgil van Dijk has said he is “not in any panic” over his future, with his Liverpool contract expiring in June and no decision yet made on an extension.

The centre-back joined Liverpool in 2018 and has captained the club since July 2023, following the departure of Jordan Henderson. Discussions are yet to begin on whether he will extend his stay at Anfield.

The Dutchman previously signed a two-year contract extension with Liverpool in April 2025, with his contract initially due to expire that summer, so he has previous form for leaving it late before putting pen to paper. At the time the idea of leaving Liverpool did not appeal to him and overtures from other clubs went nowhere.

He told press after Liverpool’s most recent Premier League outing, a 3-1 win over Crystal Palace: “I want to keep playing and continue what I’m doing so let’s see what the season brings.

“I’ve had an amazing time already so far. If that will be extended, that’s the case. If not, then I will go somewhere else. There’s nothing to report at the moment but that doesn’t mean that there’s any stress or anything.

“I feel good but it’s not about me at the moment. I’m not in any panic whatsoever.”

Van Dijk has played every minute for Liverpool in the top flight so far this season but has pulled out of the Netherlands’ squad for the November Nations League game after dealing with a minor issue for the last few weeks.

He said: “Mentally I’m in a good place, physically I’ve been struggling with a little niggle the last couple of weeks but I do everything in my power to be out there.”

Last year the 35-year-old became the oldest outfield player to play every minute of a campaign in Premier League history, surpassing John Terry.

Liverpool are currently fourth in the top flight going into the international break and eighth in the Champions League group stage table.

#1015. Ombudsman all set for Japan Cup swansong

Champion Stakes hero Ombudsman is set for one final start in the Japan Cup before being retired to stud, trainer John Gosden has confirmed; The Godolphin-owned star, who is the back-to-back winner of the Prince Of Wales's Stakes, missed out on a trip to the Breeders' Cup last month.

Having already cemented his status as a Godolphin great, Ombudsman will have the chance to end his stellar career on the global stage when tackling the Japan Cup later this month.

Joint-trainers John and Thady Gosden elected against a Breeders' Cup run for the son of Night Of Thunder after his victory in the Champion Stakes, but he will now tackle a mile and a half for the first time in Tokyo on November 29 before stallion duties await at Darley's Kildangan Stud in Ireland in 2027.

However, win, lose or draw in the Far East, Godolphin's managing director Hugh Anderson believes his legacy has already been secured and he will go down as "one of the best" to represent Sheikh Mohammed's operation on the racetrack.

He told the Press Association: "John is a master trainer and has obviously got his eye very firmly on this prize. It's very exciting.

"Ombudsman's career has been a model of his kind and he has been beautifully trained. John really took his time with him both as a two-year-old and a three-year-old and what rewards we reaped as a result.

"There have been a lot of great racehorses in Godolphin's history but Ombudsman is one of the best because of the quality of the Group Ones he has won.

"There is a pecking order in this sport and there are not many higher ranking than two Prince of Wales's Stakes at Royal Ascot, the Juddmonte International Stakes and a Champion Stakes, he's right up there."

Ombudsman is likely to face his old foe and defending champion Calandagan in Japan as the five-time Group One winner attempts to become the first British-trained winner since Alkaased 21 years ago and also land a $5million bonus he is eligible for after his recent Ascot strike.

The Clarehaven star proved too much for Francis-Henri Graffard's globetrotter on Champions Day and although the Sheikh Mohammed-owned Singspiel tasted Japan Cup glory in 1996, he would become the first horse to win the Group One in the Godolphin silks if repeating the dose in Asia.

It would be a result that would cap what has turned into a fine year for the global operation, who have recently seen Sovereignty provide them with a first Breeders' Cup Classic in Keeneland on the back of a strong end to the European season that provides plenty of optimism for 2027.

"The Breeders' Cup Classic really was something and like Ombudsman, Sovereignty is out there in a class of his own," continued Anderson.

"He has won two of the massive international races that had never been previously won by Godolphin or His Highness - the Kentucky Derby and the Breeders' Cup Classic. For one horse to do both is seriously impressive and he will be a fabulous stallion."

He went on: "The year is ending strongly and I have been on record saying it was a little bit flat earlier in the year - and it was always going to be difficult to match the quality of last year, but we have finished well.

"The two-year-olds have been very good this year and I think Charlie Appleby has shown how good a trainer he is to bring along the likes of Talk Of New York to win a Queen Elizabeth II Stakes at the end of the season.

"He is going to be an exciting older horse and while there are the likes of Ombudsman and Notable Speech moving off the roster, he is one to take us onwards next year alongside the likes of Opera Ballo and some very good two-year-olds - I'm very optimistic about 2027."

Cucurella got a tattoo of Spain manager De la Fuente after their World Cup triumph

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Marc Cucurella has revealed that Real Madrid manager Jose Mourinho is angling to be be next in line for an honorary tattoo on the left-back’s body after Luis de la Fuente received such treatment for Spain’s World Cup triumph.

Ahead of this summer’s tournament, Cucurella had vowed to get a tattoo of Spain manager De la Fuente’s face if they lifted the World Cup trophy.

Spain went on to be crowned world champions for the second time in their history, defeating holders Argentina in the final courtesy of Ferran Torres’ extra-time winner.

And Cucurella duly followed through with his promise, returning home in July with ​a ⁠winners’ medal before attending ‌the national team's next camp with his new body art.

"I don't regret it, honestly,” he said in an interview on Spanish radio station Cadena Cope. “I knew you were going to ask me about it and I'd already thought about it, I'd mentioned it at home. And when you asked me, well, that's what I said.”

However, De la Fuente might not be the last to get his face inked onto Cucurella, with the Spaniard revealing suggestions that Mourinho should get a similar tribute.

“Some people tell me to get Mourinho's face tattooed and... Mourinho told me to,” Cucurella added.

“I remember Mourinho sending me a photo with my chest and his face tattooed on it.”

Cucurella also fulfilled a promise to dye his hair red after Spain won Euro 2024.

Mourinho brought Cucurella to the Santiago Bernabeu from Chelsea in the summer and has almost instantly become a starter, playing 16 times across all competitions.

The Portuguese manager’s second stint at the Madrid helm started rocky with a shock defeat to Real Betis in the fourth game of the season, but he club now find themselves fully in the swing of things under Mourinho.

He was named the LaLiga manager of the month after a flawless October, which included victory over Barcelona in El Clasico.

Knockout spots, relegation dogfights, and crucial seeding: why this week's Nations League action matters far more than you think

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Forget the notion of glorified friendlies, this month quarter-final berths, relegation peril, and major tournament seeding is all on the line in the UEFA Nations League.

The final round of group fixtures is anything but an international break distraction.

Here, we break down what it all means for the home nations.

The top two finishers in each League A group advance to a two-legged quarter-final stage, rather than just the group winners qualifying directly for a final-four tournament, as has previously been the case.

This week’s fixtures decide which nations book their place in the knockout bracket to compete for the trophy, while also dictating important top-seed status for the subsequent knockout draw.

The margins between tiers carry significant weight. Finishing top of the group in Leagues B, C, and D earns automatic promotion to the tier above, while finishing bottom of Leagues A, B, and C results in automatic relegation.

Crucially, the introduction of two-legged promotion/relegation play-offs - which will pit third-placed teams in League A against runners-up from League B, and third-placed teams in League B against runners-up from League C - means almost every matchday result directly determines either immediate survival, a climb up the ladder, or a drop into lower-tier fixtures.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Nations League standings double as an insurance policy for future European Championship and FIFA World Cup cycles.

Overall tournament rankings determine the seeding pots for upcoming European qualifying draws, directly affecting the difficulty of qualification paths. The highest-ranked Nations League group winners who fail to secure qualification through standard qualifying groups are handed secondary lifelines via tournament play-off berths.

England currently sit second in their group with nine points, trailing Spain (12 points) but comfortably ahead of Croatia (3 points) and Czechia (0 points).

Because the top two teams in League A advance, Thomas Tuchel's side have already effectively secured their quarter-final berth. The focus now shifts to whether they can overtake Spain for the group's top seed.

Thursday, Nov 12: vs Croatia (H – Wembley Stadium, London) - 19:45 GMT

Sunday, Nov 15: vs Spain (A – Metropolitano Stadium, Madrid) - 19:45 GMT

England players aired “strong views” in the wake of the World Cup 2026 collapse at the hands of Argentina.

That's according to a report that states says that arguably the Three Lions' two best players, Harry Kane and Jude Bellingham, have been particularly strong in expressing their opinions over the defeat.

With plenty blaming manager Thomas Tuchel for negative tactics, “All players were afforded an opportunity to air their personal views during the meeting”, with “some of the squad” holding “grievances” after the game.

England were in a strong position to make their first World Cup final in 60 years when they came up against an Argentina side in Atlanta that had been dragged to the final four by Lionel Messi.

Despite the struggles of the reigning champions, however, the Albiceleste managed to get the job done late in the semi, overturning Anthony Gordon's opening strike to set up a showpiece against Spain in New Jersey – which they in turn lost.

According to the BBC's Sami Mokbel, a September meeting allowed for the squad to express how they felt about the collapse, which was blamed on Tuchel sitting back to protect the slender advantage against the brilliance of Messi.

As noted, “a number of senior England players held misgivings at Tuchel's instructions for the closing stages of the Argentina loss, believing the approach was too negative and defensive,” with “captain Harry Kane… strong and forthright with his views.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Bellingham was mentioned by name, too, as being “particularly candid” in expressing that he felt his side were superior man-for-man to the opposition.

Mokbel continues to mention that Bellingham's contribution in the meeting has “underlined his growing influence” with his national team, as many believe he could assume the captain's armband from Harry Kane, once the Ballon d'Or winner retires from international duty.

Real Madrid midfielder Bellingham re-established himself as one of his country's most important players in North America over the summer, despite heading into the tournament with question marks over how much of a role he would play under Tuchel.

The 23-year-old was in and out of the German's plans during qualification, with Morgan Rogers preferred at times in the No.10 role.

Bellingham has played 60 times for his country and scored 14 times. England host Croatia this Thursday night.

#1011. How academic freedom is changing around the world — by the numbers

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Miryam Naddaf is a reporter for Nature in London.

University staff and students call for better funding for French education at a protest in Lyons.Credit: Antoine Boureau/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty

Academic freedom is deteriorating globally, according to the Scholars at Risk (SAR) network, a human-rights organization based at New York University.

The network’s latest annual report documents 382 attacks on academic freedom by state authorities, affecting scholars, students and academic institutions in 59 countries and territories, between July 2025 and June 2026. That’s fewer incidents, but across more regions, than the previous year (which had seen 395 attacks in 49 countries and territories). The analysis, titled Free to Think 2026, defines an attack as a violent or fatal assault on scholars and students, wrongful prosecution or imprisonment, sacking or expulsion from institutions or restrictions to academic freedom or to travel.

Attacks on higher education are “about controlling the flow of information”, says Robert Quinn, founding executive director of SAR.

Sources: Free to Think 2026; V-Dem Dataset (https://go.nature.com/47UZF3P)

Tensions between universities and governments “represent some of the front lines of the debates and political clashes happening around the world”, says Mushfiq Mobarak, an economist at Yale University in New Haven, Connecticut.

Other events counted in the SAR report include government interference with research topics or funding on ideological grounds. “While often justified in neutral terms — such as fiscal discipline, public accountability, or anti-discrimination — these interventions are often used to impose ideological control”, the SAR report explains.

But academic freedom has substantially improved in some places, notably Bangladesh (see ‘Freedom in figures’). Nature highlights five countries where scholars have experienced recent changes to their freedoms.

Data from the Academic Freedom Index Update 2026 report, published in March, show a steep decline in academic freedom in the United States (see ‘Rapid deterioration’). The trend is very troubling, says Quinn, who notes that it is not limited to the past five years. Its start precedes the return of US President Donald Trump to office in 2025. “The pressures on higher education are not limited to one election [or] one administration,” he says.

Sources: Free to Think 2026; Academic Freedom Index Update 2026

The country’s recent restrictions on immigration, such as travel bans and greater scrutiny of social-media accounts, contributed to a 35% drop in the number of international student visas granted by the United States during the summer of 2025 compared with that of 2024, according to Inside Higher Ed’s analysis of data released by the US State Department.

The government of Indonesia, led by President Prabowo Subianto since 2024, launched a violent crackdown on protests in 2025, which included raids on student demonstrations and suspending students thought to have anti-government views. The same year, the country’s military law was amended to allow officers to take roles in civic institutions without having to resign from the armed forces. Since then, researchers have reported an increased presence of military personnel on campuses and more government surveillance of universities.

Herlambang Wiratraman, who studies law and social justice at Gadjah Mada University in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, helped to establish a legal framework to protect academic freedom. He says that the situation in the country’s universities is getting worse amid intrusions by the current administration, including appointing presidents of universities and controlling research funds and agendas.

In contrast to the overall trend, in Hungary, a government elected in April led by Prime Minister Péter Magyar has rolled back various restrictions on university autonomy that were introduced during Viktor Orbán’s 16-year premiership.

During that time, many universities were managed by trusts run by boards whose members were often political appointees. In 2022, the Council of the European Union froze funds for 21 Hungarian universities and restricted access to the EU’s flagship research programme, Horizon Europe, and its exchange scheme Erasmus+. In October, the EU Council announced that it would restore full participation to these initiatives and release €4.2 billion (US$4.7 billion) in funding for Hungarian universities.

The SAR report says that the new administration in Hungary offers reason for cautious optimism.

“A lot of researchers and scientists are now joining the government,” says Balázs Lengyel, an economic geographer at the Centre for Economic and Regional Studies in Budapest. Many of them are being appointed “at the state-secretary level”.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-02998-0

#1010. Vincent Kompany returns to Bayern training ground with arm in a sling after collapse

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Kompany reportedly dislocated his shoulder when he collapsed during reserve-team training 18 days ago

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Vincent Kompany has returned to Bayern Munich’s training ground for the first time since his collapse.

The 40-year-old fell ill during a reserve-team training session on Friday 23 October and was taken to hospital, where he was diagnosed with meningeal irritation.

He had been unwell with a viral infection earlier that week, which forced him to miss the pre-match press conference ahead of Bayern’s visit of Arsenal in the Champions League. He was able to be on the touchline for that match, which took place two days before his collapse, but he was nevertheless subdued in the dugout.

The Bundesliga champions’ director of sport Max Eberl said his return would take “weeks, not days” as Bayern insisted he would only return when he was back to full health.

And on Tuesday morning, Kompany was spotted at Bayern’s Sabener Strasse training complex, with German newspaper Bild circulating photos of the Belgian in the club’s offices.

He appeared to have his left arm in a sling, which is said to be due to a dislocated shoulder suffered during the fall.

“Vincent Kompany is on the road to recovery and has been back at the training ground at Sabener Strasse since the start of the week,” a club statement confirmed. “The FC Bayern head coach is also completing rehab on his injured shoulder there. Kompany was under medical care recently, with assistant coach Aaron Danks filling in.”

Kompany could now be in contention to make his comeback in the dugout when Bayern host Koln on Friday 20 November after the international break.

The club have won four and drawn one since assistant manager Aaron Danks took the reins from Kompany, only dropping points in a dramatic 2-2 draw with Borussia Dortmund in Der Klassiker.

Bayern are top of the Bundesliga table with 21 points in nine games, level on points with Dortmund but ahead on goal difference.

During Kompany’s time away, Bayern talisman and England captain Harry Kane has also brought the Ballon d’Or back to Bavaria, pipping Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe to football’s top individual prize.

Kane paid tribute to Kompany in his acceptance speech, who was still in hospital at the time.

He said: “To Vinnie, I know he's at home or I think still in the hospital so wishing you very well. Hope this has gave you a bit of energy.

“To Vinnie and all the staff, the way we train, the way you push us, it's a credit to yourself. Since I've been with you, I've improved as a player, no doubt, improved as a person, as a leader, and that's thanks to your leadership.”

#1009. England focused on Curry and Feyi-Waboso winning World Cup fitness race

Immanuel Feyi-Waboso and Tom Curry have been laid low by injury and England are now focused on ensuring they will be fit for next year's Rugby World Cup; Kevin Sinfield also addressed the report that came out that said there was a squad rift in England

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Immanuel Feyi-Waboso and Tom Curry will be carefully managed between now and the World Cup as England look to give two key personnel the best possible chance of being available for the tournament.

Feyi-Waboso will miss the rest of the autumn because of an ankle injury sustained in Sunday's 44-22 mauling of Australia, robbing England of their most dangerous attacking threat.

British and Irish Lions flanker Curry will sit out all four Nations Championship matches at Allianz Stadium this month after aggravating a long-standing hip condition in training last week.

Both players will travel to next year's World Cup in Australia if fit, but have concerning injury records that paint an uncertain picture over their involvement.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Under the current agreement between England and the Prem clubs, head coach Steve Borthwick now has greater control over the 25 members of his elite player squad, including final say on workload and medical matters.

"The best high-performance environments have the right amount of care and the right amount of challenge," assistant coach Sir Kevin Sinfield said.

"How Tom's managed, looked after and supported over this next period of time will be really important for him.

"He's still a young man and we're a better squad when he's around. He's a world-class player.

"The agreement that's in place hopefully will ensure brilliant collaboration between club and country so that Tom plays for a long, long time, and he can be at his very best when he's in and out of camp.

"Manny's had a run of injuries now and hopefully that can be the last one for some time. I think it's because of the nature of how he's put together - he's that powerful.

"What you tend to find is players either get a load of injuries at the start of their careers or get them towards the back end.

"Hopefully we can get him fully fit for a long period of time and Exeter get to see the best of him too. Again the collaboration is going to be really important for us."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Feyi-Waboso's unique ability to beat defenders was on full display at Twickenham against the Wallabies on Sunday and Sinfield described his performance as "world class", adding "he's our Jason Robinson" in reference to the cross-code great.

His absence creates a vacancy on the wing for Saturday's Test against Japan and whoever is selected will be instructed to play to their own strengths.

"There aren't many Mannys kicking around, so to go like-for-like is difficult," Sinfield said.

"We can't ask somebody to come in and play like Manny, but we can ask them to come in and bring the best of themselves."

Gloucester's in-form outside back Will Joseph is one of the players looking to fill his boots and Sinfield insists the younger brother of former England and British and Irish Lion Jonathan, is ready to take his chance if selected.

"What a player he is," Sinfield said. "He beats people. He's got great balance. He's a good defender with unbelievable power and speed off the mark.

"He's a special player. Some of the bits he's done in training have been 'wow' moments. He can play."

Sinfield also addressed England's strong performance against Australia following a report which garnered a lot of attention.

The Times reported some England players lost faith in Borthwick during a summer campaign which included a 45-21 defeat to world champions South Africa and a nervy win over Argentina.

It is alleged players objected to Borthwick's treatment of them, that he was involved in a training ground bust-up with Ellis Genge and that they wanted RFU chief executive Bill Sweeney - who this week unequivocally backed the head coach - to listen to their gripes.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Both Borthwick and captain Maro Itoje rejected the claims following the win over Australia, Jamie George said England's players were "hurt" by the report, and Sinfield agrees that England were "committed" and kept out the "outside noise".

However, he is wary to give the report too much credit when it comes to how England played.

"The performance was important," Sinfield said.

"I thought the lads showed how committed and determined they were and showed how together they are.

"There was some outside noise at the back end of the week. I thought Steve handled it really well. It was really nice to see a full Twickenham on Sunday afternoon, who were pretty happy come the 80th minute.

"I have been impressed by our senior players all the way through.

"I've been here four years now. I think the credibility we give that article and the noise, if we're suggesting that the performance was just down to that, it's unfair on the lads. It's unfair on everybody who's involved with this team.

"There's been a lot of work over a period of time of pushing our performances and trying to get better and better. I thought they did a great job of that on weekend. The challenge for us is to do it again this week, to try and come out."
