It was SpaceX's 125th launch of the year.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

SpaceX just launched a classified mission for the U.S. military.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base this evening (Nov. 6) at 7:48 p.m. EST (4:48 p.m. local California time; 0048 GMT on Nov. 7), rising into the sky as the sun sank toward the Pacific.

The launch kicked off the USSF-432 mission for the U.S. Space Force, which we know little about. Neither SpaceX nor the Space Force told us much about USSF-432 beforehand, and we learned tonight; SpaceX cut its webcast off about 10 minutes into the flight, shortly after the Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth for a landing.

That touchdown occurred aboard the SpaceX droneship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed downrange in the Pacific Ocean. It wrapped up the eighth flight for this particular booster, which is designated 1095.

The Falcon 9's upper stage, meanwhile, continued carrying its mystery payload skyward. It could be headed to low Earth orbit, outside observers speculate.

"It is possibly a batch of classified LEO satellites for the USSF's Space Based Sensing and Targeting (SBST) portfolio based on SpaceX's Starshield satellite bus, based on locations of rocket stage drop zones being exact fits with previous Starlink Group 15 launches," NextSpaceflight.com wrote in a mission description.

Starlink is SpaceX's LEO broadband megaconstellation, which consists of more than 11,000 active satellites. Starshield is a similar system designed to provide services to the U.S. military and its allies. Starshield satellites are believed to be based heavily on the Starlink spacecraft bus.

USSF-432 was the 119th Falcon 9 launch of 2026, and the 14th national-security flight of the rocket so far this year. The vast majority of Falcon 9 missions in 2026 — more than 70% — have been devoted to building out the Starlink megaconstellation.

SpaceX has also launched six other missions this year. Three were operational flights of the company's Falcon Heavy rocket, while the other three were test missions of its next-gen Starship vehicle. SpaceX plans to retire both the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy shortly after the fully reusable Starship, the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built, is up and running.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

#891. Kane and Bellingham air strong views in England World Cup review

Kane and Bellingham made their views clear at the review

England players are understood to have aired strong views about their World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina in a team meeting.

As BBC Sport reported in September, the Football Association (FA) process included canvassing the opinions of the squad - and it has emerged that took place at a 'full and frank' meeting with head coach Thomas Tuchel at the start of the September international break.

BBC Sport has been told the squad feel that now they have been able to have their say, they can move on from their heartbreak in Atlanta on 15 July.

And this was demonstrated in the last international break when England, after a narrow defeat by Spain in the first game, went on to win the next three matches impressively.

Burn replaces injured Guehi in England squad

Is Palmer's England career over under Tuchel?

'A beautiful story' as Bellingham brothers called up

The ramifications of the Argentina defeat, or perhaps more pertinently, the circumstances, meant some of the squad held grievances, with those feelings lingering and even growing throughout the summer.

In particular there was unhappiness about how Tuchel told them to approach the closing stages of the game after Anthony Gordon had given them a 55th-minute advantage.

Enzo Fernandez struck an equaliser with five minutes left, before Lautaro Martinez headed in a stoppage-time winner.

As reported by BBC Sport at the time, a number of senior England players held misgivings at Tuchel's instructions for the closing stages of the Argentina loss, believing the approach was too negative and defensive.

Hindsight, of course, is 20/20. England appeared to retreat in the closing stages of the last-16 tie against Mexico earlier in the tournament - but successfully defended a 3-2 lead to reach the quarter-finals to trigger scenes of joy at the iconic Azteca Stadium.

Nevertheless, certain players felt let down by the team's apparent pragmatism during the closing stages of the loss to Argentina amid a sense that going for the South Americans' jugular would have provided greater success.

Inevitably, the game against Argentina emerged as a key theme at the squad discussion.

It is understood that Tuchel pointed to the quality of the opposition as a key factor on why they eventually succumbed to two late Argentina goals.

There is, of course, merit to that argument. Lionel Messi was in the opposition team after all.

That said, it was not an argument the players in the meeting were prepared to universally accept.

There is a strongly held view within the England squad that their team, man-for-man, was superior to Argentina, who had 38-year-old Nicolas Otamendi on the field for the closing 18 minutes of the game.

All players were afforded an opportunity to air their personal views during the meeting.

As you would expect, captain Harry Kane was strong and forthright with his views.

Jude Bellingham, too, is said to have been particularly candid in expressing his belief that this current crop of England players were more than capable of continuing to take the game to Argentina.

Bellingham's contribution to the meeting is said to have underlined his growing influence within the England squad, with many believing the Real Madrid midfielder will become the team's captain once Kane is no longer in the picture.

If the air needed to be cleared after the World Cup then it appears those honest discussions at the end of September did the trick.

Barring the 3-2 defeat by Spain at Wembley in their first Nations League fixture in September, England have bounced back from the loss to Argentina emphatically - scoring 12 goals without conceding in three fixtures against the Czech Republic and Croatia.

Similarly, the fluctuating relationship between Bellingham and Tuchel seems to have improved, too.

"It was a bit of an up and down [relationship] of course but we are in a good place," Tuchel said last week.

"I love to be his coach. He's a top player, a very influential player and I think it goes both ways."

We will get a clearer idea of how 'Tuchel 2.0' is progressing in the next few days when England host Croatia on Thursday and travel to Madrid to face world champions Spain on Sunday.

#890. How Kelly Clarkson Helps Daughter River Navigate "Hard" Junior High

The Voice’s Kelly Clarkson shared insight into parenting her daughter River Rose, 12, as she navigates school, friendships and conflict during an exclusive E! News interview: "Junior high sucks."

Kelly Clarkson's daughter is spreading her wings and learning to fly above the drama.

As her and late ex-husband Brandon Blackstock's 12-year-old daughter River Rose experiences the ups and downs of junior high school, the Voice coach shared how she took a chance, made a change and guided the tween to break away from the woes of adolescence.

"I'm a pretty progressive parent, so I'm like, 'No, no. You're gonna make your own mistakes, and that's OK,'" Clarkson told E! News' Will Marfuggi in an exclusive interview on The Voice season 30 live show red carpet on Nov. 9. "I'm not like an 'I told you so,' but I do implement advice."

"They're growing up," she continued. "One's in junior high, and junior high sucks. It's a hard age with friends, and arguing and stuff like that. I do offer advice, and I've had my daughter come back and be like, 'So you were right.'"

But the 44-year-old—also mom to 10-year-old son Remington Alexander with Blackstock—will always help her daughter stand a little taller, even when she doesn't heed her mom's warnings.

As she explained, "I've had them be like, 'OK, so I didn't do that, and I should have.'"

While Clarkson is hitting all the right notes of motherhood, she's also had a pitch-perfect time on The Voice alongside fellow coaches Adam Levine, Queen Latifah and Riley Green.

Although the Maroon 5 frontman took home gold last season with Alexia Jayy, he couldn't wait another minute to focus on this season.

"He doesn't really brag like that," Clarkson said. "He's not that guy. I totally would. I'd be like, 'Good luck,' just for fun or whatever. But he's pretty chill about it."

But the "Breakaway" singer would be lyin' if she said she wasn't looking forward to working with Latifah and Green as the newest additions experience the live rounds for the first time.

"What's amazing about Queen is she's such a legend," Clarson emphasized. "I know people throw around the term legend a lot, but she actually is. She's done so much, be it Broadway and movie musicals, be it rapping, be it singing, be it acting, whatever it is. She's just always doing stuff."

Simply put, "That brought just a legendary kind of status to the show for us this season."

Meanwhile, the "Worst Way" singer has definitely brought more than wine and roses to the singing competition.

"Riley is just currently crushing it on the charts, like everywhere," she continued. "His career is blown up. It's a different point in his career for him, too. So it's fun. They're bringing that different energy of what's happening in their world at this chapter in their lives."

While fans wait to see who wins big during The Voice season 30, press the red button and keep reading for surprising secrets about the series.

Does the winner of The Voice get any money?

The winner of The Voice is promised a recording contract with Universal Music Group, the monetary value of which is technically unknown.

But while NBC and series producers have never confirmed any amount, the last singer standing at the end of the competition reportedly gets $100,000.

Past winners have acknowledged getting paid, season 18 champ Todd Tilghman telling People in 2020, "I don't have any immediate plans to make any drastic changes tomorrow. I don't know for sure the direction my life will go in. There's a possibility that that money might pay the bills for a little while."

But, he added, since his wife had promised their kids a trip to Disney World, he guessed he'd be splurging on that too.

Not that the value of the music opportunities that open up for the winners should be discounted.

“I’ve got a catalog of songs. I have a lot of writer friends I want to collaborate with," season 27 winner Adam David of Team Bublé told Parade in May 2025. "The plan is to put out some music and go on to work. We’re going to put out some music, and we’re going to hit the road."

How does an aspiring contestant get to The Voice's Blind Auditions?

In addition to individual recruiting (such as when producers reached out to Frenchie Davis eight years after she was on American Idol), The Voice traditionally held in-person auditions around the U.S. Lately, however, the talent search is online, judges holding virtual open calls and weeding through video submissions to find singers who then may get a chance to sing for the coaches in hopes that at least one of them turns around.

Contestants must be at least 13 years old when they embark on their audition journey. The hopefuls have 90 seconds to introduce themselves and sing. They can sing anything they want but, per the show's FAQ page, they're encouraged to pick a tune "that best suits your voice and represents you as an artist."

Judges listen to auditions for "five or six days with approximately 18 to 20 auditions per day," executive producer Audrey Morrissey told SheKnows in 2018. Once they're selected for the blind round, she explained, "Artists are with us for several days prior to [their audition] to rehearse with our band, work with wardrobe/styling and camera block on the audition stage."

Then there's the filming to put together the packages introducing some of the hopefuls and their families, all of which came as a surprise to season six alum Ddendyl Hoyt. "I had no idea that reality TV was filmed kind of like a drama," she told the Washington Post in 2014, “So everything is filmed in segments and that’s kind of the longest process of it all.”

How many times can you audition for The Voice?

If at first you don't make it out of the untelevised rounds—or onto a team if you do make it to the blind auditions—you're free to try out as many times as you want, albeit only once per season.

"I can't be a mean judge," coach Reba McEntire, who won season 25 with Asher HaVon, told Newsweek in 2023. "It's good just to say, 'If you want to come back again, try it again next season, maybe a song that suits you, one that you're really comfortable with and that really shows your talent,' give them advice and encourage them to come back."

As of season 28, there's also the Carson Callback card to be played, in which longtime host Carson Daly grants an aspiring artist who didn't get any takers another shot.

Do The Voice contestants get to pick out their own clothing?

The show has a massive wardrobe department that ensures the contestants take the stage in elevated fashion—once they've made it onto a team.

"We shop for each artist to come up with great looks," Morrissey told SheKnows. "Once we get to the live shows, looks are customized for each specific performance."

How much time do the coaches really spend working with The Voice artists?

The celebrity coaches might not be pulling all-nighters, but they're invested in getting their teams ready for the battle rounds and beyond.

"The coaching sessions take place over four days," Morrissey said, "and the actual battle performances take two days."

Meanwhile, she added, how involved a coach gets with each artist "depends on the coach. Some love a big production and like working out all the details…Other coaches mainly focus on the music and arrangement for the performance."

Some coaches "are avid texters while others email," Morrissey added. "All off-camera interactions intensify as the artists move through the competition and the stakes get higher."

But it takes a village, former contestant Hoyt telling the Post, "What they don't show is all the coaching that comes from the staff: The vocal coaches, the band director, the producers, everyone has notes for you."

Snoop Dogg told Access Hollywood in September 2025, "The behind-the-scenes people don't get the credit that they deserve. It's a lot of people, moving things, making it happen…All of these people back here that make our job easy, all we gotta do is walk onstage and do what we do."

Who picks the songs the contestants sing on The Voice?

Between coaches and artists, Morrissey said, “The No. 1 communication is about song choice.”

The artists can theoretically offer their two cents when it comes to picking their songs, but usually the coaches rule on that front.

Season one's Frenchie—who competed under O.G. coach Christina Aguilera's tutelage—told Cosmopolitan in 2021 it was "always hysterical when the judges say, 'I don’t think that was a good song choice for you,' and I'm thinking, you picked that song.”

On the flip side, season 24 winner Huntley credited coach Niall Horan with helping him find his way, telling NBC Insider the One Direction alum "knows how to pick songs, I'll tell you that."

What sort of resources are available to help The Voice artists tend to their mental health?

Aspiring contestants are screened beforehand to see if they seem emotionally ready for the pressure that lies ahead, and then the show employs mental health professionals to help the artists both during and at the end of their journey.

“We had to start visiting to check on our well-being," season six alum Kat Perkins told Cosmopolitan of the counselors on staff. "The minute you are eliminated, you walk from that stage and into the psychiatrist’s office for a debriefing. They make sure that you talk about it. It’s very needed because you’ll never go through anything like it again. It’s traumatic and you’re not really emotionally set up to do something that big that quickly."

How do the chairs on The Voice really work?

The coaches are masters of their own domains, the big red chairs evolving over the years but always boasting the ability to turn around at the push of a button. In 2018 they received a sleek upgrade, including the addition of three more buttons—giving each coach the chance to block a fellow coach, once per round, from getting a chance at claiming the contestant behind the voice.

Not unlike a luxury car seat, in addition to an automobile-caliber aluminum frame and shiny paint job, each chair has self-adjusting heaters ("Me and Reba, we're the butt-warming kings," Snoop quipped to Access Hollywood) and dual cupholders (as requested by former coach Blake Shelton).

But, according to Perkins, the dramatic whoosh sound the chairs make when they turn around is added in post-production.

"You almost don’t notice it," she told Cosmo, "especially when you’re focusing and singing to the crowd that’s in the studio."

While congenial ribbing between coaches is part of the show's DNA, it was unclear at times over the course of the 16 seasons they were on The Voice together if Blake and Adam Levine were as exasperated with each other as they seemed.

"We are constantly at each other's throats, and sometimes we really do get mad at each other," Blake told The Tennessean in 2017. "We're those two guys you knew in high school where we have this bond that is unexplainable. It brings out the best and worst in both of us. It truly is an explosive relationship. And I know every trick to get under his skin."

Translation: "He's one of the best friends that I have, but I still want to kill him sometimes."

And even though they haven't competed against each other since 2019, Adam knows what the fans want.

"The Voice season 1 after party, at my house with dips--t @blakeshelton," the O.G. coach captioned a throwback pic ahead of his return to the show in February 2025 for season 27.

Meanwhile, subsequent crops of coaches were far less likely to tweet out each other's private phone numbers.

"You spend so much time together," Niall said during an NBC sit-down, "and I was hoping it wasn't going to be like this TV relationship where the cameras go around and we're like [feigning enthusiasm], 'Hey, Snoop Dogg!' I was always nervous about that, doing the show in the first place. I just didn't want it to be like a forced relationship, and it hasn't been that at all."

#889. Keira Knightley Reveals Which of Her Movies She’s Only Seen Once

Keira Knightley—who played Juliet in the 2003 film Love Actually—revealed she’s only seen the Christmas classic one time: “I think I’m the person that knows it the least of anybody.”

If you look for it, you'll find that Keira Knightley’s love for Love Actually isn’t, actually, all around.

After all, the 41-year-old—who played Juliet in the 2003 rom-com—revealed she’s only seen the film once.

“I have not watched Love Actually since the premiere, which was when I was 18,” she told Heart in a video shared Nov. 9. “So, I think I’m the person that knows it the least of anybody.”

And before you go asking her what could be worse than the total agony of being in love, just know there’s a high chance she’ll have no idea what you’re on about.

“I know that people have a particular look on their face and then they say things to me and I know that means they’re quoting Love Actually,” she explained, “but I don’t really know what it is. It means nothing to me.”

Plus, it doesn’t help that the Pirates of the Caribbean actress’ time on set was so short.

“It was a week when I was 17,” she noted. “So, I don’t remember it, really.”

Even so, she’s proud of the film’s legacy.

“I quite like that it has this life,” she added. “Such a big life out there.”

The Richard Curtis-directed Christmas classic follows a slew of interconnected love stories in London during the weeks leading up to the Dec. 25 holiday. And while some characters in the film get the s--t kicked out of them by love, Knightley’s Juliet finds herself in a love triangle with her husband Peter (Chiwetel Ejiofor) and his best friend Mark (Andrew Lincoln).

The situation comes to a head when Mark shows up on Christmas to profess his love using cue-cards. And while the scene has cemented itself as one of the most unforgettable rom-com moments in history, the Pride & Prejudice star previously revealed she and the film’s director worked hard to make sure the grand gesture didn’t seem "stalker-ish" for viewers.

“My memory is of Richard, who is now a very dear friend, of me doing the scene, and him going, ‘No, you’re looking at [Andrew] like he’s creepy,’" she told Variety in 2024. "And I’m like, ‘But it is quite creepy.’"

That’s why Knightley changed up her facial expression to try to improve the scene, recalling that she continued by “having to redo it to fix my face to make him seem not creepy.”

For more proof that Love Actually secrets really are all around, read on…

1. Love Actually opens with scenes of travelers hugging and kissing their nearest and dearest as they reunite at London's Heathrow Airport."This is my favorite bit in the film, in fact," writer/director Richard Curtis said in a director's commentary version of the film. "This footage was shot by a hidden camera, which was in Heathrow Airport for a whole week."And the movie's team really had to jet to get permission to use these clips of real-life passengers."Every time they saw something they really liked, then the runner would charge off and ask the people to sign a bit of paper, whether or not they were happy that it should be shown in the film," he continued. "I still think it'll be quite a surprise to the people who go to the cinema and see themselves."As for the inspiration behind the scene, it came from Curtis' personal experience."I got stuck in an airport in L.A. for an hour and a half waiting for a package, and I just saw all these people just all hugging and kissing," he added. "And you realize that behind normal people in the park and in the street, there's all these stories of love."

2. The first character fans meet in the 2003 movie is Bill Nighy's Billy Mack. He's a rock and roll star approaching his golden years who releases a holiday cover of Wet Wet Wet's "Love Is All Around," which secured the No. 1 spot in the U.K. for 15 weeks after the release of Curtis' 1994 film Four Weddings and a Funeral.While it can be hard to imagine anyone but Nighy playing the part, he wasn't initially in the running for the role. It wasn't until the actor stepped in to help with a table read that Curtis knew he was the one for the job."I had two famous guys in mind to play the aging rocker Billy Mack, and I couldn't decide who to ask," the filmmaker told The Guardian in 2013. "But at the read-through, Bill did it so perfectly he became a definite yes. I've never told anyone else who I wanted. I'll put it in my will."

3. Martin Freeman has also shared his casting story. In Love Actually, he portrays a man named John who meets a woman named Judy (Joanna Page) while they're stand-ins for a movie and filming a sex scene. They have great conversations, go out on a date and fall in love.At the time of casting, Curtis had fallen in love with the U.K. version of The Office, which Freeman starred on from 2001 to 2003."I got attached to Love Actually because on the back of The Office Richard Curtis wrote me a very nice and flattering letter that contained a piece of chocolate in it," The Hobbit star recalled to Vanity Fair in 2020. "It was like a wrapped chocolate presented to me saying, 'I love The Office. I love what you did in The Office. It was amazing.'"

4. Before Thomas Brodie-Sangster was cast as Sam—a British boy who loses his mom and turns to his stepdad Daniel (Liam Neeson) to help him navigate his crush on American schoolmate Joanna—Joe Alwyn tried out for the part."This local community center where I took fencing lessons, this brilliant U.K. casting director called Shaheen Baig, she came around and she saw me there," The Favourite alum and ex of Taylor Swift, shared on a 2018 episode of Live With Kelly and Ryan. "It meant that I got time off school to go to this audition, so I went to it."In fact, Alwyn said he went through several rounds of auditions and "a whole series of workshops" before the filmmakers decided to go with Brodie-Sangster."I didn't get it in the end, obviously," he added, "but I do remember meeting Hugh Grant and Richard Curtis and sitting down and reading some scenes."

5. Colin Firth played Jamie, a writer who leaves London for his French country home after learning his girlfriend cheated on him with his brother. There, Jamie meets Portuguese housekeeper Aurélia (Lúcia Moniz). And while they don't speak the same language, they understand the feelings they've formed for each other.Jamie returns to England for a family Christmas party only to turn back around and, after learning some Portugese, propose to Aurélia. As he leaves, his niece yells, "I hate Uncle Jamie." And apparently, the name was a playful jab at Curtis' brother."Richard only called colin firth's character 'jamie' so the kids could say 'I hate uncle jamie,'" his wife and script writer Emma Freud tweeted in 2015. "His brother is called jamie."6. As for Aurélia, Curtis shared in the director's commentary the name was a nod to a friend-slash-employee who looked after his and Emma's son.7. In one scene, Jamie types outside while Aurélia clears a cup that had been holding down his papers, resulting in the wind sweeping them into a lake. Curtis said they used a wind machine so loud the lines were dubbed.Aurélia dives in to retrieve the pages, and Jamie follows. However, Curtis said the lake was only 18 inches deep at the time of filming."They're kneeling now, pretending to swim, but actually crawling along the bottom, the poor things," he added in the commentary. "And Colin got stung by a sort of animal and his elbow swelled up to the size of three avocados the next day."

8. Martine McCutcheon played Natalie. Her character joins the staff of the newly elected prime minster David (Grant), and the two develop a crush on each other.Curtis knew McCutcheon was the one for the role right from the get-go."I wrote Martine McCutcheon's part for her, too," he told The Guardian. "I even called the character Martine, though I had to change it before the read-through so she didn't think she'd already got it."

9. One of Grant's most famous scenes is when he does a celebratory dance to The Pointer Sisters' song "Jump (For My Love)" after standing up to the U.S. president. However, the actor wasn't thrilled about having to bust out some moves."I think I saw it in the script," Grant said in 2022 for The Laughter & Secrets of Love Actually: 20 Years Later – A Diane Sawyer Special, "and I thought, 'Well I'll hate doing that.'"In fact, Curtis said Grant "kept saying no." Still, the Notting Hill star gave in eventually."He was grumpy," Curtis added in the special. "It was a contractual obligation, a bit of contractual obligation acting."As for his reaction to Grant's performance in that scene?"I’m thinking, ‘Oh, good he’s doing it,'" he recalled. "Two, that’s agonizingly embarrassing.”And Grant admits he was off with his lip-synching and dancing."I'm out of rhythm by the way," he told Diane Sawyer, "especially at the beginning when I wiggle my ass.”However, Grant is willing to take a bow for the scene's ending."It was my idea to have the secretary lady catch me," he noted in the special. "Genius!"

10. While it's clear Laura Linney's character Sarah had a crush on her co-worker Karl (Rodrigo Santoro), it wasn't as obvious to viewers that the costars were navigating their own heartaches off-screen."Hands down, I got the best kiss. Sorry!" the actress said on a 2019 episode of The Graham Norton Show, referencing Sarah and Karl's make-out session that ends when she receives a call about her brother Michael's mental health battle and leaves to be with him. "And it was sweet because we were both very brokenhearted when we made that movie. He had just been dumped, I had just been dumped."Linney recalled how she and Santoro were "slumped in the van" lamenting about their breakups while on their way to film the scene."I turned to him, and I said, 'Well all day long we get to make each other feel better,'" she remembered, "and I think there is a sweetness to the scene because of that. We were both very sad."

11. Fans certainly said "I do" to the scene where Keira Knightley's charater Juliet marries Chiwetel Ejiofor's Peter, especially the part where the couple walks down the aisle and are surprised by musicians popping up from the church pews to perform The Beatles' "All You Need Is Love."While the wedding is a joyful part of the film, the inspiration for it actually came from a day of mourning: Jim Henson's funeral, which Curtis called "the most moving thing" he's ever attended."At the end of it, Frank Oz was talking and he suddenly lifted up Kermit's puppet and started to sing this song called 'One Voice,'" he explained in the director's commentary. "And it turned out all the guys in the memorial service had brought their puppets with them, and they lifted them up. And when you turned around and looked backwards, there were 50 puppets all singing. And Big Bird walked down the aisle of St. Paul's Cathedral, and they all came forward and just this massive chorus of puppets all singing. It was an extraordinary thing. So, this was our little stab at that."

12. After the wedding, Juliet visits Peter's best friend Mark (Andrew Lincoln) to see if he captured any video footage of the wedding day. While she was under the impression he hated her, she learns (after popping in a VHS tape featuring footage of only her at the wedding) that he's actually been shielding his romantic feelings for her. In the scene, Juliet wears a hat. However, Knightley explained there was a reason for this fashion choice.

“I got the biggest zit of my life when we were shooting this scene,” the actress told Jimmy Fallon on a 2019 episode of The Tonight Show. “And this scene is the important one, isn’t it? It was like another head growing out of my head."While Knightley said the makeup and lighting departments tried to hide the pimple, it was no use."There was nothing they could do," the Pride & Prejudice star added, "so the hat went on."

13. Fast-forward to later in the movie, Mark shows up at Juliet and Peter's house and rings the door bell. When she answers, he instructs her to tell her husband it's carol singers. Mark then comes clean about his love for her through a series of cards, including one that says "To me, you are perfect." In fact, Lincoln actually wrote out the cards himself.

"It is my handwriting!" The Walking Dead actor told Entertainment Weekly in 2013. "It’s funny, because the art department did it, and then I said, 'Well, can I do it?' because I like to think that my handwriting is really good. Actually, it ended up with me having to sort of trace over the art department’s, so it is my handwriting, but with a sort of pencil stencil underneath."Juliet and Mark then part ways after she gives him a controversial kiss goodbye. In a 2017 sequel short for Red Nose Day, it's revealed that Juliet and Peter are still married and that Mark has tied the knot with supermodel Kate Moss, who was featured on one of his cards in the OG film.

And that wasn't the only notable memory from shooting the romantic moment. Knightley also recalled having to redo her reaction to his cue card reveal a few times so that the gesture seemed less "stalker-ish."

In a December 2024 interview withVariety, she detailed changing up her facial expression to try to improve the scene, saying she wound up “having to redo it to fix my face to make him seem not creepy.”

14. While there appears to be a bigger age gap between Knightley and Brodie-Sangster in the movie, they're only five years apart IRL. She was 17 when they made the film, and he was 12.

15. Brodie-Sangster really did learn how to play the drums for Love Actually, in which his character picks up the instrument to impress his crush Joanna (Olivia Olson) at their school's Christmas concert."I did learn to play the drums for it,” he told The Sunday Post in 2017. “My dad’s a drummer and he taught me in my grandad’s basement bashing away on his old kit and trying to play along to 'All I Want For Christmas [Is You].'”16. And yes, that really was Olson singing the Mariah Carey hit."Everyone thinks she is lip-synching, and she was 9 or 10 years old," screenwriter Freud said at the Montclair Film Festival in 2016, per the event's recap of her presentation, "but that was her.”17. What's more, the scene where Joanna gives Sam a peck on the cheek at London's Heathrow Airport before she flies back to America marked her first on- and off-screen kiss.

"I was really nervous because I kind of had a crush on Thomas back in the day," the actress told E! News in 2016, "and I was also worried because I was taller than him."The kiss clearly left an impression on both characters. In the 2017 Red Nose Day special, it's revealed that Sam reconnected with Joanna in New York and that they got engaged—with them flying back to London to ask Neeson's character Daniel for his blessing.

18. Another unforgettable scene is when the character Harry (played by the late Alan Rickman) is trying to buy a necklace for his secretary Mia (Heike Makatsch) without his wife Karen (Emma Thompson) knowing, but the jewelry salesman Rufus (Rowan Atkinson) is moving at a snail's pace.And apparently, the Mr. Bean star was in no rush to finish filming the scene.

20. One of the most heartbreaking parts of the movie is when Karen finds the necklace in Harry's coat pocket, thinks it for her and then unwraps a Joni Mitchell CD for Christmas instead—leading her to realize he bought the necklace for another woman.After she puts on a smile for their children's Christmas concert, Karen tells Harry she knows what's going on. And while fans wondered if the couple remained married, Freud solved this mystery. "They stay together," she tweeted in 2015, "but home isn't as happy as it once was."And Freud says Harry's relationship with Mia went beyond the necklace."DEFINITELY had an affair," she wrote, "i begged richard just to make it a flirtation, but no. the whole way."

21. With several other beloved rom-coms under his belt—including Four Weddings and a Funeral, Notting Hill and Bridget Jones's Diary—Curtis resurfaced a scene he'd cut in a previous film for Love Actually.The scene stars a man named Colin (Kris Marshall), who is serving hors d'oeuvres at a wedding. In a failed attempt to flirt, he strikes up a conversation with a woman and tells her how bad the food is—except it turns out the woman is the caterer."This highly amusing scene coming up now about catering with this girl is a re-working of a highly amusing scene about catering, which bore remarkable resemblance down to the last line which was originally in Four Weddings and a Funeral," Grant, who appeared in both films, revealed while doing the director's commentary with Curtis, "which was one of my audition scenes, but which got cut from the final film."In fact, Curtis admitted he forgot to change the name from Charles in Four Weddings and a Funeral to Colin in Love Actually in a line of the re-worked script.22. Fed up with searching for love in the U.K., Colin decides to go to America and try his luck there. He flies to Wisconsin, where he meets a group of women at a bar, including one named Jeannie played by January Jones."January jones wrote half of her lines," Freud revealed in a tweet. "She was sooooo funny when we filmed that scene."

23. While there were several familiar faces in Love Actually, Freud revealed her and Curtis' kids also made a few cameos."THAT IS SCARLETT CURTIS THERE ON THE RIGHT," she tweeted about her daughter, who was dressed as one of the lobsters in the school's Nativity play (yes, you read that right). "NOT EVEN JOKING."In addition, she noted the boy with the crown and Spider-Man face-paint in the Christmas play is their son Jake, with her writing, "I gave birth to him."24. Looking back at the film two decades later, Curtis admits there are aspects of the film he wishes he could change."The lack of diversity makes me feel uncomfortable and a bit stupid," he admitted in the Diane Sawyer special. "I think there are three plots that have bosses and people who work for them."The director has also expressed regret over the film's comments about Natalie's weight.“I think I was behind, you know, behind the curve, and those jokes aren’t any longer funny," he told The Hollywood Reporter in 2023, "so I don’t feel I was malicious at the time, but I think I was unobservant and not as, you know, as clever as I should have been.”

25. While Love Actually features 10 different storylines, Curtis said he originally had more.

"At first, we had 14 different love stories, but the result was too long, so four ended up going, including two we'd actually shot," he told The Guardian. "One was based on a poster in Alan Rickman's office of two women in Africa. The camera actually went into the poster and heard them talking about their daughters' love lives. Another involved Emma Thompson's son getting into trouble at school and the camera following the harsh headmistress home."In the since-released deleted scenes, the headmistress can be seen heading home to take care of her partner Geraldine, who is dealing with an illness and later dies. Another deleted scene shows Sarah talking about family Christmas memories with her brother Michael. They ask each other how they're doing now. While Sarah says "everything's great," Michael gets real with her about his mental health struggles and says, "I'm in hell."Even though Curtis decreased the number of storylines, he admitted stringing the remaining ones together was no easy feat.

"Although all the strands come together in the airport at the end, it still felt like making 10 separate films," he told The Guardian. "It was a massively difficult edit. The order I originally wrote it in didn't work at all, so we had to reorder it completely. It was a bizarre four-month game of 3D chess."

#888. Incident-by-incident: Was it a bad weekend for VAR?

Manchester United's last-gasp equaliser against Aston Villa survived a VAR review for a potential foul

Whisper it quietly, but the statistics say video assistant referee decisions have been pretty good in the Premier League so far this season.

The Key Match Incidents (KMI) Panel, which looks at every contentious decision and votes whether it is right or wrong, reported just two VAR errors after eight rounds of matches.

At the same stage last season, there had been six mistakes.

Then came this weekend, during which almost every top-flight game had a controversial decision.

BBC Sport looks at most of these situations - there really were too many to do them all - and assesses the likelihood that the KMI Panel will add to the list of errors.

Man Utd grab a point in dramatic fashion late on against Aston Villa

Incident 1: Penalty awarded to Manchester United for a foul by Boubacar Kamara on Matheus Cunha in the 16th minute.

Verdict: The spot-kick was awarded because the Villa defender went through Cunha to win the ball. Replays clearly showed the first contact was on the Brazilian's foot.

What the KMI Panel might say: This will be a correct decision.

Incident 2: Possible foul by Senne Lammens on Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki before Patrick Dorgu's 96th-minute equaliser.

Verdict : There are similarities to a goal Arsenal scored at Old Trafford last season, when William Saliba leant into United goalkeeper Altay BayÄ±ndÄ±r.

Lammens was not looking at the ball, which increases the chances of a VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel might say: With the higher bar for an intervention in the Premier League, and minimal contact, it is unlikely to be a VAR error to not disallow the goal.

Why Arsenal should have been given a penalty against Hull

Incident: Kai Havertz was pulled down inside the area by Nobel Mendy. The VAR, Michael Oliver, sent referee Farai Hallam to the pitchside monitor for a penalty, but it was not given due to an offside offence by the Germany international.

Verdict: BBC Sport covered this incident in detail on Saturday. As the foul happened before any potential offside offence, the penalty should have been awarded.

What the KMI Panel might say: Even though it feels wrong to reward a player in an offside position with a penalty, the law says otherwise and this is likely to be a mistake.

Should Bogle have seen red for this challenge in the Leeds v Tottenham game?

Incident: Jayden Bogle fouled Mathys Tel, with referee John Brooks giving the free-kick but no sanction for the Leeds player. The VAR, Tony Harrington, opted not to send Brooks to the monitor for a red card.

Verdict: BBC Sport covered the merits of this incident on Saturday. It was a difficult call for the VAR, because Bogle caused the foul with his supporting rather than his challenging foot. Still, it was a very painful challenge and some believe it should have been a red card.

What the KMI Panel might say: Was it an unfortunate incident, or a tackle which endangered the opponent? This will depend upon which former players are on the KMI Panel for this week, because it has split opinion among ex-pros.

Frank Lampard post-match interview - Everton v Coventry

All three incidents were covered in more detail by BBC Sport on Friday.

Incident 1: Coventry's Caleb Yirenkyi appeared to have his hair pulled inside the area by James Tarkowski, but no penalty was awarded.

Verdict: While the interpretation on hair pulling was relaxed for this season, meaning this would not be a red card, there appeared to be a yank of the hair by the Everton defender.

What the KMI Panel might say: Incorrect decision, penalty kick.

Incident 2: Another penalty claim for Coventry as Everton's Vitalii Mykolenko clipped Taiwo Awoniyi on the edge of the box.

Verdict: Replays shows that the contact on Awoniyi was made just before the line.

What the KMI Panel might say: Correct decision, no penalty.

Incident 3: Thierno Barry put Everton in front in the 61st minute, but there was a VAR check for a potential handball.

Verdict: The VAR determined there was no conclusive evidence for a handball, yet there does appear to be a deviation and the goal probably should have been ruled out.

What the KMI Panel might say: As the VAR does not have the super-zoom - this takes a few minutes to calibrate and is not available instantly - no VAR intervention might be supported. This was the case with a goal scored by Crystal Palace against Nottingham Forest. It could be a split vote.

Igor Thiago will be suspended for three Premier League games after his VAR red card for violent conduct

Incident: Igor Thiago was sent off following a VAR review after he caught the head of Chema Andres with his forearm.

Verdict: The Brentford striker can consider himself unfortunate, as there is doubt that he truly intended to catch the Spaniard in the face.

What the KMI Panel might say: It may seem like a soft dismissal, but the VAR intervention is likely to be supported because the law does say that a strike to the head should be a red card, unless force is negligible.

'Yellow card for me' - Dublin on Thiago red card

Incident: Crystal Palace were awarded a penalty three minutes into stoppage time for a foul by Milos Kerkez on Dario Osorio.

Verdict: We saw a similar incident the 2024-25 season when Arsenal defender William Saliba headed Joao Pedro after the Brighton striker had won the ball. This was voted to be a correct penalty decision.

What the KMI Panel might say: This incident is not quite the same as Saliba on Pedro, and more of a 50-50 clash. It may be voted as an on-field error, but not to the threshold for VAR.

Incident: Cole Palmer went down on the edge of the area under a challenge from both Luke O'Nien and Jules Ahoka, and asked for a penalty. Referee Jarred Gillett did not give a foul.

Verdict: A foul is determined by the first contact on the attacker. That a player falls into the box with contact continuing would not make it a penalty. Only on holding offences is continuing contact relevant.

What the KMI Panel might say: There is no conclusive evidence that any initial foul contact happened inside the area, so no penalty is likely to be supported.

Incident: Newcastle thought they had taken the lead at Craven Cottage, only for the goal to be ruled out for a foul by Yoane Wissa on Timothy Castagne.

Verdict: Matthias Jaissle was perplexed in his post-match interview, yet he would surely be furious if a Fulham player held one of his defenders back to create on onside corridor for another attacker to score.

What the KMI Panel might say: This is likely to be voted as a correct decision.

BBC Sport estimates that there are two decisions which the KMI Panel is very likely to log as a VAR error: not awarding penalties to Arsenal and Coventry.

Two further calls, Barry's goal and the potential red card to Bogle, may be errors but will depend who is on the panel and where their subjective opinion lies.

The others on the list are likely to be correct.

So we are potentially looking at two to four errors, which is not a good weekend.

Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County star Aspyn Ovard exclusively told E! why she feels the truth about her relationship with married couple Bri and Billy Davis will take viewers by surprise.

And the influencer did exactly that by taking fans inside her relationship with married couple Bri Davis and Billy Davis while filming The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County.

"There's a lot of different arcs of my life that are shared on the show," Aspyn exclusively told E! News. "But I am excited to be representation of a different kind of relationship."

And there's a reason the 30-year-old looks forward to viewers getting a look at her life in a throuple on Hulu’s Secret Lives of Mormon Wives spinoff, premiering Nov. 12.

As she put it, "Because there's just not a lot out there, and it's easy to share for me. And I know it's not easy for everybody."

Though the YouTuber—who filed for divorce from ex Parker Ferris in 2024 after eight years of marriage—admitted exploring the new chapter of her sexuality was "a big deal" for her, fans shouldn't expect any major plot twists while witnessing her current relationship.

"I'm very curious to kind of see what people will say because I think that I've seen some crazy theories, and it's just not that crazy of a thing," Aspyn, who began sharing about her bisexuality online following her breakup with her high school sweetheart, noted with a laugh. "I think unfortunately people will be a little bit underwhelmed."

Still, the mom of three girls—Cove, 7, Lola, 5 and Elle, 2—clarified, "It was very overwhelming for me."

Ahead of Mormon Wives: OC's release, Aspyn and Bri detailed how their love story came together—including how Aspyn signaling her queer identity led to Bri reaching out.

So, when the TikToker suggested, "What if we all hung out?" referencing the nurse's husband, Bri was open to expanding their connection.

"I was like, 'I’m not opposed.' I already really like you, and I knew her vibe and her energy, and I knew Billy’s vibe and energy," Bri explained in their Oct. 11 YouTube diary. "I was like, 'They kind of match.' Like, I kind of—I can see the vision."

In addition to Aspyn's love life, the months leading up to the end of costar Jen Affleck's relationship with estranged husband Zac Affleck will unfold on SLOMW: OC. Get filled in on where all the show's couples stand ahead of the premiere.

Following her divorce from Cory Althoff, podcaster Bobbi Althoff is dating Tyler Hawkins, who plays a special role in Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County.

"He styles me, that’s how he supports me,” she told E! News in May, adding that the basketball player, "picks out my outfits every day. He styles me every day for the show. It’s great."

Aspyn Ovard, who filed for divorce from Parker Ferris in 2024 after eight years of marriage, is currently in a throuple relationship with married couple Billy Davis and Bri Davis.

After many ups and downs, Jen Affleck—who is pregnant with her and Zac Affleck's fourth baby—officially filed for divorce from her husband of seven years, E! News confirmed Nov. 4.

Despite ongoing relationship speculation, Salomé Andrea and Aaron Brimhall are still going strong as they prepare to welcome their third baby together. The duo, who married in 2012, also share 8-year-old twins Luca and Rue.

McCall DaPron—the sister of Mormon Wives' Mayci Neeley—shares four kids with husband Kirk DaPron, who she wed in 2011.

Ashleigh Pease and Nate Pease are rock solid after over a decade of marriage. "This 13th year together is one that has felt full circle!" she wrote on Instagram in September. "A season of fruits. Comfort. The happiest milestones."

"I think the implications are pretty severe, which is why we're taking it so seriously and putting such extreme focus on the mission right now."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman is serious about launching "big rockets" to the moon every single year for the agency's Artemis program. And the new space race with China is fueling that ambition.

"I feel good. I feel like we are certainly on a more achievable path to the lunar surface today than where we were before," Isaacman told Space.com.

We recently sat down with the NASA chief to discuss the state of the Artemis program, and, off the bat, he made it clear that he's confident in the U.S. space program following the success of April's Artemis II mission around the moon. In fact, just prior to our conversation, it was announced that Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman will become the new deputy director of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. But the road from Artemis II's success to crewed lunar landings and, later, a permanent moon base will take a lot of launches of NASA's Space Launch System (SLS) megarocket, Isaacman stressed.

"You know, a lot of people, especially in the space community, start getting [into] if the landers are there or not. I don't really care about that right now. What I care about is that we are launching big rockets no less than once a year," he said.

"I think that's imperative for NASA to be doing these deep-space human spaceflight missions right now," Isaacman added. "So, we had a great mission in April of '26. We will launch again in '27."

That coming launch will be for Artemis III, a crewed mission to low Earth orbit that will test docking procedures between NASA's Orion capsule and one or both of the Artemis program's private lunar landers — SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon.

"We need to continue to exercise those muscles," he said, referring to SLS liftoffs. "And, honestly, once a year isn't great, either. I mean, I don't think we're going to get back to the early [space] shuttle days, you know, four missions a year. I don't think we're going to get back to where we were with Apollo, but once a year is the minimum … I would testify that to Congress in this role years down the road.

"If NASA is going to be doing deep-space missions, complicated missions, [we should] launch at least once a year and get as much out of it as you can for taking the risk and spending the taxpayer dollars and building towards something greater," Isaacman added. "That's what we're doing with Artemis III, and that's what's going to better prepare us for Artemis IV."

So, how is NASA coping with the challenges that face them as they approach Artemis III ahead of a crewed lunar landing on Artemis IV, which is targeted for 2028? While NASA can learn some lessons from past moon missions with Apollo, today it's primarily relying on the extensive experience and talent within the agency, according to Isaacman.

"Artemis II is very different from Apollo 8, and Artemis III will be very different from Apollo 9," he said. "Our approach is not exactly the same as it was … But what is the same right now? The spirit, the energy, the potential within NASA. The talent of the workforce and industry is no different than the 1960s."

There's another similarity to the Apollo era: NASA has a rival in its race to the moon. While the adversary in the 1960s was the Soviet Union, today the U.S. is competing against China.

"It is a real space race," Isaacman said. But, he added, "this one is very different than the first one."

"Everything is closer than it was, not just in space. I mean, we had the edge in computing [and] every one of the technology domains during the Cold War. Our capabilities were better by a mile," he said. "[But with] China, it's not [like that]. They're very close."

"We're saying we're going to land on the moon at the end of 2028. China is saying by the end of 2029," Isaacman added. "And it's like, Well, are they going to pull it off? Yes, they will. They've showcased their landers, their rovers, their suits, two-launch architecture with built-in reusability."

So NASA is taking the Chinese threat very seriously, according to Isaacman.

"The consequence of getting this wrong, I'm telling you — it's going to be felt around the world," he said. "It will call everything into question."

"Should I be using American superintelligence or AI? Should I be doing Chinese? Should I be buying their computers? Should I be [buying] ours? Buying their cars, their airplanes, their ships? Whose security guarantees to trust?" Isaacman added. "I think the implications are pretty severe, which is why we're taking it so seriously and putting such extreme focus on the mission right now. But we have that playbook of success, and I think we will prevail."

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. #882. Manchester City’s weaknesses under Enzo Maresca are being exposed

After three straight defeats, City’s manager says he will use the international break to reassess. Their problems may go beyond tactics

Enzo Maresca seemed, if not quite baffled by his side’s Saturday defeat to Nottingham Forest, then at least a little put out. After seven straight wins from the start of the season, that’s now three straight defeats, a pattern so unusual that it’s been recorded only once before in top-flight English history, by Sheffield Wednesday in 1904-05. The three defeats were all different, Maresca said, although in all of them City had had more possession and more chances.

In the 2-1 defeat at Aston Villa two weeks ago, City had 63% of the ball and had 15 chances to Villa’s eight. In the 1-0 home defeat to Brighton last weekend, they had 62% possession and 21 chances to seven. At the City Ground, it was 79% possession and 12 chances to 11. So Maresca is right in one way: City could look at basic statistics and say they had been unfortunate – although Forest could equally point to the fact that they went into that game third top of the expected goals table but second-bottom of the actual table.

But there is another statistic that should concern Maresca: City have not kept a clean sheet since their victory at Anfield after the last international break, nine games ago. And the game before that, they let in three against Sunderland. In those last eight games, City have conceded 17 goals. It’s true that three of those can at least in part be blamed on errors by Gianluigi Donnarumma, but there are also structural issues. City have a vulnerability in transition that Forest ruthlessly exploited, a weakness not unfamiliar to Maresca’s teams. One of the criticisms he received at both Leicester and Chelsea was that his sides were often extremely cautious in possession, but that makes sense given how high a line he likes to play.

That’s also why duels are so crucial to his teams; losing possession immediately exposes a high back four. Maresca was visibly disappointed at the way City were outfought in the first half against Forest. Lose the ball and the opposition has a run at a back four with space behind it. That is always going to be a problem but especially so when the opposing center-forward is a Liam Delap who has just remembered how to play and is determined to make somebody pay for a year and a bit of disappointing form.

Yet the midfield Maresca picked was clearly vulnerable to being outmuscled. He clearly rates Enzo Fernández extremely highly, to the point that City paid £125m ($167.7m) to sign him from Chelsea. But Fernández, for all his gifts as a footballer, is not especially physical by the standards of the Premier League. When he and Cole Palmer played together, there was often a sense that it made Chelsea a little lightweight. Maresca, though, was so determined to field the Argentinian that he would come up with complex tactical solutions, such as using Malo Gusto as a weird right-back-cum-No-10 hybrid.

City are running into similar problems. Rayan Cherki is an enormously gifted attacking midfielder, but not one who can be relied upon defensively, either in terms of his positioning or his willingness to make tracking runs, something Pep Guardiola acknowledged last season. He can be physically outmatched. That is not necessarily a huge problem with two mobile runners behind him: ideally an Elliot Anderson-style shuttler and a more defensive holding and/or ball-winning presence like Rodri. But Rodri has gone and Fernández leaves Anderson with a huge amount of the physical work to do. If Anderson happens not to be on the spot – if, say, a defender loses the ball in a dangerous area, or a break bypasses him – City are very quickly exposed.

Maresca said he will use this international break to reassess, that this was a rare example where it was better for a team not to have another game straight away to try to put a defeat behind them. Perhaps there is a tactical solution to be found. Perhaps even one that isn’t just: don’t play Fernández and Cherki together. But he must also be aware that by the time the Premier League returns, City could be out of the title race, or effectively even out of the Premier League itself.

It was during the last international break that the independent panel announced City had been found guilty of all but one of the charges brought against them by the Premier League. There is a school of thought that the sanctions could be announced during this international break. It’s all but impossible, of course, to know precisely how it’s affecting players to play under the cloud of a potential huge points deduction, but if initial defiance has faded into a sullen acceptance, that may also lead to battles being lost, to a lack of intensity and desire.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

The issue is tactical, but it may not only be tactical.

#881. Managerial 'inconsistency' hurting Ghana - Hughton

Kim Bjorkegren (right) is in interim charge of Ghana after Carlos Queiroz left the Black Stars by mutual consent

As Ghana prepare for two make-or-break 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) qualifiers with women's coach Kim Bjorkegren in temporary charge, former boss Chris Hughton has called for greater consistency in the Black Stars dugout.

The West Africans face Somalia in back-to-back fixtures over the next week, having lost their first two games in Group C against Ivory Coast and The Gambia last month.

Those defeats resulted in the departure of Carlos Queiroz, whose brief period in the hot seat was characterised by uncertainty.

The Portuguese's exit means Swede Bjorkegren, who has been in charge of the Black Queens since January 2025, has now been asked to lead the men's team against Somalia.

"When you have inconsistency in the amount of time when a manager is staying, it's never good," Hughton told BBC Sport Africa.

"You want that consistency in the players [and] the players want that consistency in what they see in the manager."

Queiroz, who had two spells as Sir Alex Ferguson's assistant at Manchester United, was initially appointed in April and led Ghana to the last 32 of the Fifa World Cup, holding England to a goalless draw in the group stage, before announcing his own departure shortly after the team were eliminated 1-0 by Colombia in the last 32.

However, the 73-year-old was reappointed in early September, with the Ghana Football Association (GFA) praising his "extensive international experience" gained during time in charge of South Africa, Egypt, Portugal, Iran, Colombia, Qatar and Oman.

But Queiroz's return lasted less than a month following a 2-0 defeat by the Ivorians in Bouake and a 4-2 humbling against the Gambians in front of home fans in Accra.

"What I saw in the World Cup is that they represented the country very well, particularly the England game," said Hughton.

"And although it was very much a defensive outfit, there were opportunities to score."

Hughton, however, admits that regular sackings can create an "attitude" within a squad, with players knowing that "if he (the coach) doesn't do well then he won't be there".

Ex-Brighton boss Hughton reveals cancer diagnosis

Ex-Brighton boss Hughton backs mental health drive

Ghana suffered group-stage exits at the 2021 and 2023 Afcons under Milovan Rajevac (left) and Chris Hughton (right) before failing to qualify for the 2025 edition under Otto Addo (right)

Hughton's Ghana reign was also short lived.

Appointed as technical director by the GFA in February 2022, he moved into the head coach role in February 2023 but lasted less than 12 months before being sacked in January 2024 after his team failed to get out of their group at the 2023 Afcon in Ivory Coast.

The former Ireland full-back, who won two FA Cups and a Uefa Cup with Tottenham Hotspur and coached Newcastle, Norwich and Brighton in the Premier League, is one of five men who have taken on the Ghana job in the past six years.

Charles Akonnor, Milovan Rajevac, Otto Addo and Queiroz are the others, with the chopping and changing further illustrated by the fact that Addo had two spells in charge during that time.

Kwesi Appiah, the current Sudan boss, lasted 33 months during his second stint with the Black Stars between April 2017 and January 2020 - the longest anyone has managed since legendary Afcon-winning coach Fred Osam-Duodu in the late 1970s and early 80s.

With Ghana in real danger of missing out on a second successive Afcon finals, Hughton believes the situation has been exacerbated by under-investment and what he describes as "fearsome" competition across the continent.

"Many years ago Ghana were at a level that was, if not the best team in Africa, certainly right up there," said the 67-year-old.

"You've seen the emergence of so many other good African nations that have made the competition levels that much higher.

"Some of these countries have so many other problems, but I do think that there needs to be an injection of government money into the structure and into the system."

Hughton feels more needs to be done to encourage the development of the game in the West African nation.

"In Ghana, the local game that used to produce so many good players, the support level is not there," he said.

"They're playing on pitches that are not of a great level and the supporters are not coming.

"The supporters in Ghana love the Black Stars most, first and foremost, and of course the Premier League is massive there, but there isn't that support for the local game that there used to be.

"I think the government needs to do more as regards putting money into the infrastructure."

Coventry City midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi scored the only goal as Ghana beat Panama at the World Cup in June

While Ghana have failed to make it past the second round of Afcon since 2017, the country's World Cup record is far more impressive.

They have qualified for five of the past six finals since their debut in Germany in 2006, reaching the knockout stage on three occasions including a quarter-final appearance at the 2010 tournament in South Africa.

Having cruised through qualification for this year's World Cup in Canada, Mexico and the United States, losing only one of 10 games as they topped their group under Addo, Queiroz could reasonably claim he was hamstrung by multiple withdrawals ahead of his first Afcon qualifiers.

Six players named in the original squad, including Antoine Semenyo, Mohammed Kudus, Jordan Ayew and Baba Rahman, dropped out, followed subsequently by some of those called up as replacements.

Hughton hopes it is a situation which is not repeated - and which was not caused by the uncertainty around Queiroz's position.

"Whether that was a reason or not, I don't know. And I probably don't think so," he stated.

"You always want your best players and it's always a concern to the level of the group when you have so many players pull out.

"There isn't too much you can do about that [and] you have to work around that."

With the team's chances of reaching next year's Afcon in East Africa in serious peril, a lot rests of the shoulders of interim coach Bjorkegren.

As Ghana's long wait for a first continental title since 1982 continues, finding some long-term stability in the Black Stars' coaching set-up would be a good first step.

*Chris Hughton was speaking to BBC Sport Africa at the Best of Africa Awards

#880. Partick Thistle lose SWPL points for amateur player payments

Partick Thistle have dropped from eighth to ninth in the 10-team table

Partick Thistle have been deducted three points and fined Â£6,000 by the Scottish Women's Premier League for making payments to players who were registered as amateurs last season.

Thistle finished sixth last season and the points penalty means they slip one place to second bottom spot, three points behind Spartans, in the current 10-team table.

It follows a hearing on Monday at which the Glasgow club were found to be in breach of rules about making payments to amateur registered players and "submitting incorrect information regarding the submission of the certificate and undertaking document required as part of the membership criteria process".

Half of Thistle's fine is suspended until the end of season.

Thistle had the right of appeal but said on their website that the club "acknowledges and accepts the verdict".

They add: "The circumstances which led to the breach of SWPL player rule 37 and competition rule E31.11 were a result of a failure of internal process, which has since been addressed and resolved so that it can not occur in future.

"The club admitted the breach immediately when brought to our attention.

"We apologise to our fans for the mistake and its consequences."

Bottom side Aberdeen are now only four points behind Thistle.

#879. Football comes together across Spain to honour Jesús de Miguel: ‘We’ve seen how fragile life is’

Across La Liga and beyond this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them

In the final few minutes before stepping into the arena once more, heading out for his 199th Osasuna match on Saturday evening, the man who has scored more first division goals than anyone in their history stopped his teammates for a moment and told them what it meant to wear the shirt. “This is very important,” Ante Budimir began as the dressing room, their sanctuary, fell silent around him. “We don’t have this shirt today for the sake of it. He was not chosen, and nor are we. It could have happened to anyone, anyone. Let us go knowing that we’re grateful to be on the pitch: playing, watching, warming up, sitting on the bench, whatever it may be. Boys, we were not chosen: not us, not him. Let us go, gratefully. Without thought. We have a grand day before us.”

With that, Osasuna’s players turned left out of the room, where they were joined in the tunnel by footballers from Athletic Club, rivals from the north, and together they went out past the little shrine of Saint Fermin on to the field. They carried white lilies and all wore the same white shirts with a No 9 on the back, a black ribbon and the name of Jesús de Miguel, the Tenerife striker who died after a collision on the pitch five days earlier at the age of 30. At almost exactly the same time, 2,000km away to the west, Tenerife’s squad were walking out at the Heliodoro Rodríguez López in Santa Cruz. They did not have anyone alongside them, wore black suits not white shirts and did not have a game to play either, not this week.

Two days earlier Tenerife had been in Navahermosa, La Mancha, the tiny village their teammate’s family are from, carrying the coffin of the friend their captain called “our Demigol”. They were supposed to be in Granada on Saturday; instead, they were back on the island, in their home ground, to say goodbye and pay homage. Publicly, this time. Lilies had been laid on the pitch there too, a Tenerife shirt with them, and a stage built at one end. “We’ve seen how fragile life is,” the captain, Enric Gallego, said, offering words he said could never be enough, carrying the burden for all of them. “We think of the journeys, the wins, the losses, and hold on to those moments that seemed normal, but that now … a few days ago we shared that with you. To talk of you in the past tense is unfair. None of us are prepared to live what we’re living through.”

No one ever could be. Across Spain this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them. That, Budimir had told his teammates, was something they must think about but not think about too. The players’ union in which De Miguel had a role, a footballer there for others, had asked for the competition to stop. Respect demanded that it did, they said, requesting a judge intervene when the league did not hear them. But it had gone on. The only matches postponed were those involving Tenerife; Andorra, whose goalkeeper Jesús Owono had crashed into De Miguel; and Castellón, who he had taken to the second division, delivering them to segunda for the first time in 16 years and himself for the first time at all, aged 27.

On the eve of the game that opened this weekend’s fixtures, the Sevilla head coach, Luis García, said he thought they should wait. It was too soon, too raw, too theirs. His midfielder Giorgi Kochorashvili had missed training the day before: a former Castellón player, Kochorashvili had asked permission to go to the funeral, leaving early and returning late, his mind elsewhere. Of course he could, García had replied, “we are humans above all else”. And it was not just him. García had worked with Owono – “let’s not make two victims, we have had enough; he is in hell, for sure”, he had pleaded – and now he said: “If there’s a play that’s similar … what do I say to my goalkeeper?

“We need time,” García had said. “We need to reflect.”

Instead, they played. From Seville on Friday night to Madrid on Sunday, via stadiums everywhere. It was, some suggested, the best way to pay homage to De Miguel but no one truly knew. “We can’t ask him what he would have wanted,” José Mourinho said before Madrid went to Valencia and won 3-0, Tenerife’s flag flying at half-mast at Mestalla. He might not have wanted anything at all. “You never wanted any attention,” Gallego said, but this weekend he was on all their minds.

“Forever in our memories,” the league’s line read. At every game in the first and second divisions, the ritual was repeated. Teams came out together wearing the same white shirts bearing his name. Flowers were laid, a little uncomfortably, on the spot inside the centre circle where he had fallen and there was a minute’s silence, players and officials gathered around the wreath. As they stood before Cádiz-Oviedo, tears ran down the cheeks of the Tenerife-based referee Marta Huerta de Aza. On stadium screens, an image of De Miguel appeared. On television screens, a QR code did: a link to a crowdfunding campaign for the young family he left, set up by the former Tenerife player Fran Sol.

The games began and then, in the ninth minute or as near as the referee could manage, they paused again: the teams stopped, looking up to the screen, where a video of his best moments played out. It was not always an easy watch, and some preferred not to.

At Sevilla, where fans saw Antonio Puerta collapse on the pitch and pass away, applause still offered in the 16th minute every game, Kochorashvili stood by the bench, eyes lost somewhere his mind was not. At Espanyol, where in the 21st minute they applaud Dani Jarque, the captain who died during a pre-season tour and to whom Andrés Iniesta dedicated the winning goal at the 2010 World Cup final, Álex Calatrava and Álvaro González, teammates at Castellón and Tenerife respectively, looked about to break. In the ninth minute at the Metropolitano, the place was still rocking, the timing out of sync: Giuliano Simeone had just scored, so the referee Javier Alberola Rojas allowed a couple of minutes to pass, choosing his moment, Diego Simeone helping him impose silence on the stands when he finally stopped it. Then they started again, expected to carry on regardless.

In Pamplona, Alejandro Catena, who scored the late equaliser in a 1-1 draw with Athletic, raised an Osasuna shirt with De Miguel’s name and number on the back. Theirs was the game that felt most out of place, attention drawn from where it should have been, where it was. It would not be true to say that it did not matter, the Osasuna head coach, Jagoba Arrasate, admitting he had been carried along with it like everyone else, the calmness he thought they had found in the months out of the game soon abandoned again.

As they played, grateful for the grand day that they had before them, all the days they did, the tribute continued in Tenerife. The Heliodoro had filled early, access by every gate except eight and nine, engulfed by flowers and candles. De Miguel’s shirt lay on the turf where he had, lilies to one side, a spotlight on it. Another wreath occupied the bench. A giant shirt stretched across one end where the stage was, a lectern awaiting the speakers. A cross presided over it. Staff and players wore No 9 badges on their lapels. Supporters came in Tenerife shirts. And in the yellow shirts of rivals Las Palmas, whose president and captain Kirian, who had recovered after cancer, came. “This is the Canaries I want,” said Tenerife’s majority shareholder, Rayco García.

In the seats set up on the pitch, Tenerife’s players and De Miguel’s family sat, their eyes heavy. The archbishop, Eloy Alberto Santiago led a mass. The club’s president and majority shareholder spoke. He promised they would never allow María, De Miguel’s widow, to be alone. He also announced they would adopt Carla, his 14-month-old daughter, supporting her economically until she is 18. Gallego addressed her, football as family meaning something. “I hope one day you can look back and see who your dad was, be proud of him, not just for the footballer he was but the person: for his humility, his goodness,” he said.

Sniffing, his voice breaking, the captain paid homage to his teammate, his strike partner, his friend. The kind of person, he said, who did not seem to be there, and definitely did not demand that people notice he was, but always was. A man, he noted, so disinclined to put anyone out that when his car broke down he walked home from training rather than bother anyone for a lift. That, he insisted, might not seem like much, but it said much. “Today we don’t want to talk only of the player; we want to talk about you, Jesús, about the person that was behind the shirt,” he had begun. “Above any game, any team, what really remains is the person and the impact you leave. And you were a very special person.”

Gallego gave way to the archbishop, orations led by Tenerife staff, and as the act came to a close, difficult days ahead, the spotlight taken elsewhere, the drums began and the fans belted out a familiar tune, once more with more meaningful than ever before:

double quotation markWe have to sing with even more strength if you’re losing Even those who left us sing, from heaven This will never stop We will sing to eternity.”

Then Tenerife’s players departed. They have training on Monday and next week they play.
